title: How Turkish Works
explanation:
Before you start learning vocabulary and grammar, it helps to understand a few key ideas that make Turkish very different from English. Once you know these principles, almost everything else will make much more sense.

1. Turkish is agglutinative.

This is probably the biggest difference from English. Instead of using many separate words, Turkish adds a series of suffixes to the end of a word. Each suffix has one clear job: it might show plurality, possession, location, tense, or many other meanings.

Think of Turkish words as being built with LEGO blocks:

ev = house

evler = houses (ev + -ler = plural)

evlerim = my houses (ev + ler + -im = my)

evlerimde = in my houses (ev + ler + im + -de = in)

Another example:

kitap = book

kitaplar = books

kitaplarınız = your books

kitaplarınızdan = from your books

At first these long words may look intimidating, but they're actually very logical. Once you learn the meaning of each suffix, you simply combine them like building blocks.

2. Word order is Subject–Object–Verb (SOV).

English usually follows Subject–Verb–Object:

I eat the apple.

Turkish puts the verb at the end:

Ben elmayı yerim.

Literally: I the apple eat.

Another example:

Ayşe kitabı okuyor.

Literally: Ayşe the book is reading.

As you learn Turkish, you'll naturally get used to waiting until the end of the sentence to hear the action.

3. Turkish uses vowel harmony.

Suffixes don't always have one fixed spelling. Their vowels change to match the last vowel of the word they attach to, making words easier and more natural to pronounce.

The simplest example is the plural suffix:

  • ev → evler (houses)
  • şehir → şehirler (cities)
  • araba → arabalar (cars)
  • çocuk → çocuklar (children)

Notice how the suffix becomes -ler after front vowels and -lar after back vowels.

Some suffixes have four different forms instead of two:

  • evim = my house
  • kapım = my door
  • gözüm = my eye
  • köyüm = my village

Don't worry about memorising every rule immediately. After seeing enough examples, vowel harmony quickly starts to feel natural.

4. There is no grammatical gender.

Unlike many European languages, Turkish nouns are not masculine or feminine.

The pronoun o can mean:

  • he
  • she
  • it

For example:

O geliyor.

Depending on the context, this can mean:

  • He is coming.
  • She is coming.
  • It is coming.

This makes Turkish grammar much simpler because you never have to memorise the gender of nouns.

5. Turkish has no articles.

English uses a, an, and the. Turkish doesn't.

Ev büyük.

Depending on the situation, this can mean:

  • The house is big.
  • A house is big.
  • House is big (rare literal translation).

The context tells you which meaning is intended.

6. Turkish pronunciation is very regular.

One of the nicest things about Turkish is that words are almost always pronounced exactly as they are written.

Unlike English, there are very few surprises.

For example:

  • merhaba is always pronounced the same way.
  • kitap is always pronounced the same way.
  • güzel is always pronounced the same way.

Once you've learned the Turkish alphabet, you'll be able to read almost any new word aloud, even if you've never seen it before.

That's the foundation of Turkish.

Everything you'll learn from this point builds on these simple ideas. Turkish may look unfamiliar at first, but it's an extremely logical language. Learn the word roots, learn the suffixes, and you'll soon be able to understand and build surprisingly complex sentences.

title: Personal Pronouns
explanation:
Personal pronouns tell us who is doing an action. Turkish has six basic personal pronouns:

  • ben — I
  • sen — you (singular, informal)
  • o — he / she / it
  • biz — we
  • siz — you (plural, or singular formal/polite)
  • onlar — they

Unlike English, Turkish does not distinguish between "he", "she", and "it". The single pronoun o can mean all three, and the context tells you which one is intended.

Siz has two uses. It means you all when talking to several people, but it is also the polite way to address one person, similar to the formal "you" in many European languages.

One important feature of Turkish is that pronouns are often left out. Turkish verbs already show who is performing the action, so the pronoun is usually unnecessary.

For example:

Gidiyorum. = I am going.

Geliyoruz. = We are coming.

You can still add the pronoun for emphasis or contrast:

Ben gidiyorum. = I'm going.

Biz geliyoruz. = We're coming.

As you learn Turkish, you'll notice that native speakers frequently omit pronouns because the verb already makes the meaning clear.

title: Nouns & the Subject
explanation:
This is the very first lesson in the chapter, so there's no earlier sentence to build on — we're starting from scratch with a single word: "The man" — "Adam." Before we can talk about what a sentence does, we need to talk about the words it's built from, starting with the most basic building block of all: the noun.

A noun is a word for a person, place, thing, or idea. "Man" is a noun — it names a person. So are "dog," "city," "book," and even something you can't touch, like "happiness." In Turkish, "adam" (man) is a noun too, and it works the same way: it names a person.

  • man
    "adam" (a person)
  • city
    "şehir" (a place)
  • ball
    "top" (a thing)
  • happiness
    "mutluluk" (an idea)

Now, once you have a noun, you can build a sentence around it, and that brings us to the subject: the person or thing the sentence is about — usually who or what is doing something. In "The man..." — "Adam..." — "the man" / "adam" is set up to be the subject, because everything that follows in this chapter is going to describe what he does.

A simple test for a subject: ask "who or what is this sentence about?" Whatever answers that question is your subject.

  • The dog barks.
    who/what is this about? → "the dog"
    "Köpek havlıyor." ("köpek" = dog)
  • The city is big.
    who/what is this about? → "the city"
    "Şehir büyük." ("şehir" = city)
  • Ayşe is smiling.
    who/what is this about? → "Ayşe"
    "Ayşe gülümsüyor."

Nouns also come in singular (one) and plural (more than one) forms. In English, you usually add "-s": "man" → "men" (irregular!), "dog" → "dogs," "city" → "cities." Turkish marks plural too, but with a suffix instead: -lar/-ler, chosen by vowel harmony. So "adam" (man, singular) becomes adam + lar = "adamlar" (men) — note that this is "adam" with a suffix attached, not a separate word; "köpek" (dog) becomes köpek + ler = "köpekler" (dogs), using -ler because "köpek" has front vowels. You'll get a full lesson on how to pick -lar vs -ler later — for now, just notice that Turkish plurals are built by adding a piece onto the base word, the same way many of its other endings work.

  • The man walks.
    "Adam yürüyor." (singular)
  • The men walk.
    "Adamlar yürüyor." ("adam" + -lar, plural)

Finally, nouns split into two kinds: common nouns, which name general people/places/things ("man," "city," "dog"), and proper nouns, which name one specific, particular person, place, or thing, and are capitalized ("Ahmet," "Istanbul," "Turkey"). Turkish follows the same split, and also capitalizes proper nouns:

  • common: "the man" — "adam"  |  proper: "Ahmet" — "Ahmet"
  • common: "the city" — "şehir"  |  proper: "Istanbul" — "İstanbul"

One extra note for later: Turkish proper nouns keep their capital letter even when a grammatical suffix is glued onto them — for example "İstanbul'a" (to Istanbul) uses an apostrophe to separate the suffix from the name. You'll meet that rule properly in the lesson on cases with proper nouns.

title: Verbs & the Minimal Sentence
explanation:
In the lesson before this one, you met the subject — the person or thing a sentence is about: "The man." ("Adam.") But "The man" by itself isn't really a sentence yet — it's just a noun sitting there. Something is missing: what is the man actually doing?

That missing piece is the verb — the word that tells you the action or state the subject is involved in. Add one, and suddenly you have a real, complete sentence:

The man throws.
"Adam atıyor." ("at-" = to throw; here as at + -ıyor, the "throwing is happening right now" ending — more on this in the present-tense lesson)

"throws" / "atıyor" is the verb here. It's doing the real work of the sentence: it tells you what's happening. Notice something important: subject + verb is already enough to form a complete, grammatical sentence, in both English and Turkish. You don't need anything else — "The man throws" stands on its own, even though it clearly invites a follow-up question (throws what? — that's for the next lesson).

A simple test for a verb: ask "what is happening?" or "what is the subject doing / being?" The word that answers that question is your verb.

Verbs come in two broad flavors. Most verbs describe an action — something the subject actively does:

  • The dog barks.
    "Köpek havlıyor." ("havla-" = to bark; here as havla + -ıyor, with the final -a dropped before the ending)
  • The child runs.
    "Çocuk koşuyor." ("koş-" = to run; here as koş + -uyor)

But some verbs describe a state or simply link the subject to a description, rather than an action — these are sometimes called "being" verbs, and the most important one is "to be":

  • The man is tall.
    "Adam uzun." — here Turkish doesn't even use a separate word for "is"! The state of being is built right into the sentence, with no verb showing on the surface at all. You'll get a full lesson on this "to be" pattern (called the copula) later, since it works quite differently from English.
  • The soup is hot.
    "Çorba sıcak." ("çorba" = soup; "sıcak" = hot; again, no separate "is")

So both "throws" and "is" count as verbs, even though one is an action and the other just describes a state — both tell you what's going on with the subject.

Verbs like "throws" also raise a question: throws what? A verb that can't stand comfortably alone without answering a question like that is heading toward needing a direct object (the very next lesson). But plenty of verbs are perfectly complete without ever needing one — these are called intransitive verbs. Compare:

  • The baby sleeps.
    "Bebek uyuyor." ("uyu-" = to sleep; here as uyu + -yor, with a buffer -y- since "uyu" ends in a vowel)
    complete; you'd never ask "sleeps what?"
  • The sun rises.
    "Güneş doğuyor." ("doğ-" = to rise/be born; here as doğ + -uyor)
    also complete on its own.

"The man throws," from this lesson, actually sits right on the edge — it's grammatically complete as subject + verb, but it strongly implies something is being thrown, which is exactly what the next lesson will add.

title: Direct Objects
explanation:
So far you've had a subject (who's doing something) and a verb (what they're doing): "The man throws." ("Adam atıyor.") That's already a complete sentence — but it leaves an obvious question hanging: throws what?

Add an answer to that question, and you get a direct object — the thing that directly receives the action of the verb:

The man throws the ball.
"Adam topu atıyor." ("top" = ball; here as top + -u, the direct object)

"the ball" / "topu" = the direct object. It's the thing being thrown — the action happens to it, directly.

A simple test for a direct object: ask "verb + what?" (or "verb + whom?" for people) right after the verb. If there's a clear answer, that's your direct object. A few more, in both languages:

  • She reads a book.
    reads what? → "a book" (direct object)
    "O bir kitap okuyor." ("kitap" = book) — okuyor neyi? → "bir kitap"
  • They saw the teacher.
    saw whom? → "the teacher"
    "Öğretmeni gördüler." ("öğretmen" = teacher; here as öğretmen + -i) — gördüler kimi? → "öğretmeni"
  • I closed the door.
    closed what? → "the door"
    "Kapıyı kapattım." ("kapı" = door; here as kapı + -yı, a buffer -y- is inserted because "kapı" already ends in a vowel)
  • The cat caught a mouse.
    caught what? → "a mouse"
    "Kedi bir fare yakaladı." ("fare" = mouse; no ending here because it's an INdefinite "a mouse", not "the mouse" — more on that distinction in the accusative-case lesson)

Not every verb needs a direct object. Some verbs are complete on their own (like "The man throws" was, one lesson ago) — these are called intransitive verbs. Verbs that take a direct object are called transitive. Compare:

  • The baby sleeps.
    "Bebek uyuyor."
    complete on its own; "sleeps what?" doesn't make sense. Intransitive.
  • The baby drops the spoon.
    "Bebek kaşığı düşürüyor." ("kaşık" = spoon; here as kaşık + -ı)
    "drops what?" → "the spoon" / "kaşığı". Transitive, with a direct object.

English marks none of this on the word itself — "the ball" looks exactly the same whether it's a subject or a direct object; only word order tells you which is which. Turkish works differently: notice that "topu", "öğretmeni", "kapıyı" all carry a vowel + -ı/-i/-u/-ü ending that "top", "öğretmen", "kapı" alone don't have. That's not a coincidence — it's the accusative case, a suffix Turkish very often glues directly onto a direct object (specifically a definite, specific one — "a door" vs. "the door") to mark it as such, precisely because Turkish word order is more flexible than English and can't always rely on position alone. You'll get a full lesson on exactly how and when to build that suffix later — for now, just notice the pattern, and remember: the ending is a GRAMMATICAL MARKER, not part of the word's dictionary meaning. "top" is the word for "ball"; "topu" is "top" doing a specific grammatical job in this sentence.

title: Indirect Objects
explanation:
In the lesson before this one, you had a subject, a verb, and a direct object: "The man throws the ball." ("Adam topu atıyor.") That covers who's acting, what they're doing, and what it's being done to. But sentences often have one more piece: throws the ball to whom? Right now, nobody's catching that ball — it's just sailing off into the void.

Add an answer to that question, and you get an indirect object — the person or thing that the action is done to or for, without being the thing directly acted upon:

The man throws the ball to the dog.
"Adam topu köpeğe atıyor." ("köpek" = dog; here as köpek + -e, with the final -k softening to -ğ- before the vowel, giving "köpeğe" — the indirect object)

Here "the ball" / "topu" is still the direct object — it's the thing being thrown. "the dog" / "köpeğe" is the indirect object — it's the one receiving the throw, the destination of the action, but the action isn't happening directly to it the way it is to the ball.

A simple test for an indirect object: ask "verb + to/for whom?" (or "to/for what?") after you've already found the direct object. Compare the two questions on the same sentence:

  • throws what? → "the ball" / "topu" — the direct object.
  • throws it to whom? → "the dog" / "köpeğe" — the indirect object.

A few more examples, in both languages, each with both objects picked out:

  • She gives the book to her brother.
    gives what? → "the book" (direct object); gives it to whom? → "her brother" (indirect object)
    "Kitabı kardeşine veriyor." ("kitap" = book; here as kitap + -ı, with -p softening to -b-, giving "kitabı" — direct object; "kardeş" = sibling/brother; here as kardeş + -i(n) + -e, giving "kardeşine" — indirect object, literally "to his/her brother")
  • I bought a present for my mother.
    bought what? → "a present" (direct object); bought it for whom? → "my mother" (indirect object)
    "Anneme bir hediye aldım." ("anne" = mother; here as anne + -m + -e, giving "anneme", "to/for my mother" — indirect object; "hediye" = present, unmarked here since it's indefinite)
  • The teacher explained the rule to the students.
    explained what? → "the rule" (direct object); explained it to whom? → "the students" (indirect object)
    "Öğretmen kuralı öğrencilere açıkladı." ("kural" = rule; here as kural + -ı, direct object; "öğrenci" = student; here as öğrenci + -ler + -e, giving "öğrencilere", "to the students" — indirect object)
  • He sent a letter to his friend.
    sent what? → "a letter" (direct object); sent it to whom? → "his friend" (indirect object)
    "Arkadaşına bir mektup gönderdi." ("arkadaş" = friend; here as arkadaş + -ı(n) + -a, giving "arkadaşına", "to his friend" — indirect object)

It's worth being careful not to mix up the two objects, since both can sit right next to each other in a sentence. The quickest distinguishing habit: the direct object is the thing directly changing state, moving, or being affected (thrown, given, bought, explained, sent); the indirect object is the endpoint — the one gaining or losing something as a result, marked in English with "to" or "for" (which can also be dropped in constructions like "She gives her brother the book," where "her brother" is still the indirect object even without "to").

English shows the indirect object mainly through word order or a preposition like "to"/"for". Turkish, once again, marks it directly on the word itself: notice that "köpeğe", "kardeşine", "anneme", "öğrencilere", and "arkadaşına" all end in a vowel + -e/-a. That ending is the dative case, and it's the standard Turkish way of marking "to/for" someone or something — you'll get a full lesson later on exactly how to attach it (including when a buffer consonant like -y- is needed, and how consonants like -k soften to -ğ- before it, as you just saw in "köpek" → "köpeğe"). For now, just remember: -e/-a at the end of a Turkish noun is a strong signal you're looking at an indirect object, not the dictionary form of the word.

One warning before you move on: this English-based direct/indirect distinction is a solid starting point, but it doesn't always predict which case a Turkish verb actually wants — the next lesson looks at exactly where that breaks down.

title: Direct vs. Indirect Objects — the Turkish Trap
explanation:
In the last lesson you learned a clean test: "verb + what?" finds the direct object, "verb + to/for whom?" finds the indirect object. That test works perfectly for English grammar — but here's the trap: when you carry that same logic straight into Turkish, it will occasionally betray you. Some Turkish verbs simply don't take the case you'd expect from the English translation.

Compare these two, side by side:

  • I see the cat.
    see what? → "the cat" (direct object, feels natural)
    "Kediyi görüyorum."
    ("kedi" = cat; here as kedi + -yi, accusative — exactly what you'd expect)
  • I look at the cat.
    English still treats "the cat" the same way — it's what you're directing your attention to.
    "Kediye bakıyorum."
    ("kedi" = cat; here as kedi + -ye, DATIVE — not accusative, even though nothing about the English sentence hints at that)

Same English pattern, same-feeling sentence — but "görmek" (to see) takes an accusative object, while "bakmak" (to look at) takes a dative one. Nothing in the English sentence "I look at the cat" warns you of this; the only way to know is that bakmak, specifically, is a verb that governs the dative case. This isn't random — it's simply a fact about that particular verb, the same way English "listen" needs "to" (you listen to music, not just "listen music") while "hear" doesn't (you just hear music). Every language has verbs like this; they just don't always land on the same side of the direct/indirect line as their English counterparts.

A short list of common Turkish "trap" verbs that take a dative object, even where the English translation feels direct:

  • bakmak (to look at) — "Resme bakıyorum."
    ("resim" = picture; here as resim + -e, dative) — "I'm looking at the picture."
  • binmek (to get on / ride / board) — "Otobüse biniyorum."
    ("otobüs" = bus; here as otobüs + -e, dative) — "I'm getting on the bus." (not "riding the bus" in the accusative sense English might suggest)
  • inanmak (to believe [in]) — "Sana inanıyorum."
    ("sen" = you; here as sana, dative form of "sen") — "I believe you." (English drops "in", making it look direct — Turkish keeps the dative)
  • yardım etmek (to help) — "Sana yardım ediyorum."
    ("sen" = you; here as sana, dative) — "I'm helping you." (English "help someone" feels about as direct as a verb gets — Turkish still wants the dative)

And for balance, a verb where Turkish and English line up exactly as you'd hope:

  • sevmek (to love) — "Seni seviyorum."
    ("sen" = you; here as seni, accusative form of "sen") — "I love you." Direct object in both languages, no surprises.

So what do you actually do with this? You can't reliably predict a Turkish verb's case just by translating the English sentence and asking "does this feel direct or indirect?" — the safest approach is to learn each verb's required case as part of learning the verb itself, the same way you'd memorize that English "depend" needs "on" (you depend on someone, not just "depend someone"). As you meet more Turkish verbs later in this course, pay attention any time a verb is introduced alongside a case — that pairing is worth learning together, as a single unit, rather than reasoning it out fresh from English each time.

title: Adjectives
explanation:
In the lesson before this one, you built up to: "The man throws the ball to the small dog."
"Adam topu küçük köpeğe atıyor." ("köpek" = dog; here as köpek + -e, the indirect object, with the final "k" softening to "ğ")
That sentence tells us who's throwing, what's being thrown, and who's receiving it. But it doesn't tell us anything about what the ball itself looks like — is it big, small, red, old? To add that kind of detail, you need a new tool: the adjective.

An adjective is a word that describes a noun — it tells you more about a person, place, or thing, like its color, size, age, or quality. Let's add one to our sentence, describing the ball:

The man throws the red ball to the small dog.
"Adam kırmızı topu küçük köpeğe atıyor." ("kırmızı" = red, describing "top" = ball; "küçük" = small, describing "köpek" = dog)

Notice "kırmızı topu" — the adjective "kırmızı" sits right in front of the noun it describes, "topu" ("top" = ball; here as top + -u, the direct object). The accusative ending -u still attaches to "top" itself, not to "kırmızı" — adjectives never carry the noun's case ending; only the noun does.

A simple test for an adjective: find a noun, and ask "what kind of [noun], or which [noun]?" Whatever word answers that question, sitting right before the noun, is your adjective. In both English and Turkish, the adjective comes before the noun it describes — this is one place the two languages actually agree in word order:

  • the small dog
    "küçük köpek"
    "small" comes before "dog"; "küçük" comes before "köpek"
  • an old house
    "eski bir ev" ("ev" = house)
    "old" before "house"; "eski" before "ev"
  • the tall man
    "uzun adam" ("adam" = man)
    "tall" before "man"; "uzun" before "adam"

What happens when you stack more than one adjective in front of the same noun? Both languages simply line them up in a row before the noun, closest-to-the-noun being the most essential description:

  • the small red dog
    "küçük kırmızı köpek"
    both "small" and "red" sit before "dog", in the same order in Turkish
  • a big old white house
    "büyük eski beyaz bir ev" ("beyaz" = white)
    three adjectives, still all stacked before "ev"

English and Turkish don't always agree on the finer points of exactly which adjective goes closest to the noun when you have several (size, then age, then color is a common English habit, for instance), but the core rule — all adjectives cluster before the noun — holds in both.

Here's a genuine simplification Turkish offers you: unlike many languages (Spanish, French, German, Russian, and others), Turkish adjectives never change form to agree with the noun they describe. No matter whether the noun is singular or plural, or what case ending it carries, the adjective itself stays exactly the same:

  • the small dog / the small dogs
    "küçük köpek" / "küçük köpekler" ("köpek" + -ler, plural)
    "küçük" doesn't change at all, even though "köpek" becomes plural
  • I see the small dog.
    "Küçük köpeği görüyorum." ("köpek" here as köpek + -i, direct object)
    "küçük" is identical to before, even though "köpek" now carries a case ending

Contrast this with English, where adjectives are almost always invariant too ("small" never changes) — so this is one grammar concept where Turkish will feel refreshingly familiar rather than harder, once you start meeting languages that do force adjectives to agree in gender or number.

Later, once you reach the lessons on Turkish noun cases and plurals, you'll see this play out constantly: the noun picks up all sorts of endings (accusative -ı/-i/-u/-ü, plural -lar/-ler, possessive endings, and more), while any adjective sitting in front of it just sits there unchanged, doing its one job of description and nothing else.

title: Adverbs
explanation:
In the lesson before this one, you built up to: "The man throws the ball to the dog."
"Adam topu köpeğe atıyor." That sentence tells you who did what, to what, and to whom. But there's still a question it doesn't answer: how did the man throw it? Fast? Gently? Carelessly? To answer that, we need a new kind of word.

That word is an adverb — a word that describes a verb, telling you how, when, where, or how much an action happens. Adverbs can also describe an adjective or even another adverb, making them a kind of all-purpose "describer of describers." Add one to our sentence:

The man throws the ball to the dog quickly.
"Adam topu köpeğe hızlıca atıyor." ("hızlı" = fast/quick; here as hızlı + -ca, turning the adjective into the adverb "quickly")

"quickly" / "hızlıca" is the adverb — it describes the verb "throws" / "atıyor", telling us how the throwing happens.

A simple test for an adverb describing a verb: ask "verb + how/when/where?" If a word answers that question, it's likely an adverb. Compare that to the direct-object test ("verb + what?") and the indirect-object test ("verb + to/for whom?") from earlier lessons — all three are different questions you can point at the same verb.

English very often builds adverbs from adjectives by adding -ly: "quick" → "quickly", "slow" → "slowly", "careful" → "carefully". Turkish has a loose parallel: the suffix -ca/-ce (with spelling and vowel-harmony variants like -ça/-çe after certain consonants) can turn an adjective into an adverb, as in "hızlı" → "hızlıca" above. It's not a perfect one-to-one match, though — many Turkish adverbs are just separate words with no suffix at all, as you'll see below.

A few more examples, in both languages:

  • She sings beautifully.
    "O güzel şarkı söylüyor." ("güzel" = beautiful; here used as-is, with no added suffix, because "güzel" already doubles as an adverb "beautifully" in this position)
  • He speaks slowly.
    "O yavaşça konuşuyor." ("yavaş" = slow; here as yavaş + -ça, "slowly" — the front vowel version of the suffix, matching the last vowel of "yavaş")
  • They arrived yesterday.
    "Onlar dün geldiler." ("dün" = yesterday; a standalone time-adverb, no suffix involved)
    this one answers when, not how.
  • The cat sleeps here.
    "Kedi burada uyuyor." ("bura" = this place; here as bura + -da, "here" — this answers where, and uses the locative case suffix you'll meet properly in a later lesson)
  • The soup is very hot.
    "Çorba çok sıcak." ("çok" = very/much; here it's an adverb modifying the adjective "sıcak" = hot, not the verb — showing that adverbs can describe adjectives too)

Notice how adverbs are more flexible in where they sit than subjects, objects, or adjectives usually are. In English, "quickly" could move: "Quickly, the man throws the ball to the dog" or "The man quickly throws the ball to the dog" — both still work, with only a slight shift in emphasis. Turkish is if anything even more flexible about word order, so "hızlıca" ("quick" + -ca) could shift around the sentence too: "Adam hızlıca topu köpeğe atıyor" is just as natural as the version above, still meaning "The man quickly throws the ball to the dog." The verb tends to stay glued to the very end of a Turkish sentence, but almost everything before it — subject, objects, adverbs — can reorder for emphasis.

It's worth contrasting adverbs with adjectives directly, since Turkish sometimes uses the exact same word for both. "hızlı" alone is an adjective ("a fast man" — "hızlı adam"), while "hızlıca" (with the added -ca) is the adverb form ("quickly"). English keeps this distinction with "fast" (which is actually both adjective and adverb — irregular!) versus the clearer pair "quick" (adjective) / "quickly" (adverb). You'll see this adjective-vs-adverb boundary again in a dedicated adjectives lesson.

Later, in a lesson on Turkish adverbs and the -ca/-ce suffix specifically, you'll learn exactly which consonants trigger the "ç" spelling instead of "c" (as in "yavaş" + -ça → "yavaşça"), which adjectives can take it at all, and which common adverbs — like "hızlı" itself when used bare, or words like "çok" and "dün" — never take a suffix and simply stand alone.

title: Pronouns
explanation:
In the lesson before this one, we had: "The man throws the ball to the dog."
"Adam topu köpeğe atıyor."
That sentence works fine, but imagine saying it over and over in a conversation — it gets clunky fast. Once everyone knows who "the man" and "the ball" and "the dog" are, you'd rather just say "He throws it to it." That shortcut is exactly what today's concept is about.

A pronoun is a word that stands in for a noun (or noun phrase) once it's already clear from context what's being talked about, so you don't have to keep repeating it. "He" stands in for "the man," "it" stands in for "the ball" or "the dog," and so on. Our running example now becomes:

He throws it to it.
"O onu ona atıyor."

Here every noun from the previous stage has been replaced by a pronoun: "the man" → "he," "the ball" → the first "it" (direct object), and "the dog" → the second "it" (indirect object).

English pronouns actually change form depending on their grammatical role — this is one of the few places English still marks case on a word itself. Compare the subject and object forms:

  • Subject: I, you, he, she, it, we, they
  • Object: me, you, him, her, it, us, them

So you say "He sees her," never "Him sees she" — the form itself tells you who's doing the seeing and who's being seen, even without word order.

Turkish pronouns behave differently: the pronoun's base stays almost the same whether it's a subject or an object — what changes is just a case suffix tacked onto the end, the same accusative and dative suffixes you've already met on ordinary nouns like "top" and "köpek". Look at "o":

  • o ("he/she/it," subject form — no suffix)
  • onu ("him/her/it," direct object)
    this is o + -nu (an extra -n- buffer appears before the accusative -u because "o" is short and ends in a vowel), NOT a different word — "o" still means "he/she/it"
  • ona ("to him/her/it," indirect object)
    this is o + -na (again with the buffer -n- before the dative -a)

So in "O onu ona atıyor," all three words — o, onu, ona — are really the same pronoun "o," just wearing different case endings depending on the job each one is doing in the sentence, exactly the way "top" became "topu" for a direct object. You'll get the full set of Turkish personal pronouns and how each one takes these suffixes in the pronoun-declension lesson later on.

A few more examples to see the pattern, in both languages:

  • I see her.
    "Onu görüyorum." ("o" = he/she/it; here as o + -nu, direct object)
    notice Turkish doesn't even need a separate word for "I" here; more on that in a moment.
  • She gives it to me.
    "O onu bana veriyor." ("ben" = I/me; here as ban + -a, the dative form of "ben," meaning "to me")
  • We help them.
    "Onlara yardım ediyoruz." ("onlar" = they; here as onlar + -a, dative, "to them" — Turkish uses the dative here because "yardım etmek," to help, grammatically takes an indirect object)

Now for a very Turkish twist. In English, you almost always need a subject pronoun — you can't just say "Throws it to it" and leave out "he." But Turkish verb endings already show who is doing the action, so the subject pronoun is often optional and gets dropped entirely. This is called pro-drop. For example, "Onu ona atıyor" (without "o" at the start) still perfectly means "He throws it to it," because the ending -yor plus the lack of any other person marker signals a third-person subject, and context fills in the rest. Compare:

  • I throw it.
    "Onu atıyorum."
    no separate word for "I" is needed; the -um ending on the verb itself says "I." ("Ben onu atıyorum" is also correct, just more emphatic, like stressing "I throw it" in English.)
  • You throw it.
    "Onu atıyorsun."
    again, the -sun ending carries the "you" meaning on its own.

So Turkish subject pronouns like "ben," "sen," "o" mainly show up for emphasis or clarity, while object pronouns (with their case suffixes) stay put much more consistently, since the verb ending doesn't tell you anything about the object. You'll see exactly how each person's ending is built in the verb-conjugation lessons coming up, where "atıyorum," "atıyorsun," "atıyor," and so on all get broken down piece by piece.

title: Prepositions & Prepositional Phrases
explanation:
In the lesson before this one, you built up to "The man throws the ball to the dog."
"Adam köpeğe topu atıyor." That sentence tells you who throws, what's thrown, and who receives it. But imagine someone asks: where did all this happen? Right now the sentence can't answer that — it's missing a piece that locates the action in space (or, just as easily, in time).

That missing piece is a preposition — a small word that shows the relationship between two things, usually place, time, or direction: "in the garden," "at noon," "under the table," "to the store." A preposition never stands alone; it always attaches to a noun (or noun phrase) to form a prepositional phrase — a unit that functions together as a single chunk of meaning. Add one to our sentence:

The man throws the ball to the dog in the garden.
"Adam bahçede topu köpeğe atıyor." ("bahçe" = garden; here as bahçe + -de, "in/at the garden")

"in the garden" is the prepositional phrase — "in" is the preposition, "the garden" is its object, and together they tell you where the throwing happens. Notice the phrase moves as a block: you could say "In the garden, the man throws the ball to the dog" and it still means the same thing, because "in the garden" travels together.

A simple test for a prepositional phrase: find the small relationship-word (in, on, at, to, under, before, with...) and everything glued to it up through its noun — that whole chunk is the phrase, and it usually answers where?, when?, or which way? about the rest of the sentence.

A few more examples, in both languages:

  • The cat sleeps on the chair.
    "Kedi sandalyede uyuyor." ("sandalye" = chair; here as sandalye + -de, "on/at the chair")
    "on the chair" answers where?
  • We arrived before dinner.
    "Akşam yemeğinden önce geldik." ("akşam yemeği" = dinner; here as akşam yemeği + -nden plus the postposition "önce" = "before")
    "before dinner" answers when?
  • The keys are under the table.
    "Anahtarlar masanın altında." ("masa" = table; here as masa + -nın, "of the table," combined with "alt" = "underside" + -ında, together meaning "under the table")
  • She walked to the market.
    "Pazara yürüdü." ("pazar" = market; here as pazar + -a, "to the market")

Here's the key structural difference to hold onto as you move into Turkish grammar proper: in English, the preposition comes before the noun — "in the garden," "to the dog," "under the table." In Turkish, that relationship is usually shown after the noun instead, either by gluing a case suffix directly onto the noun (like "bahçe" → "bahçede," "pazar" → "pazara") or by following the noun with a separate little word called a postposition (like "önce" after "akşam yemeğinden," or "önünde" after "evin" in "evin önünde" = "in front of the house"). So where English says PREPOSITION + noun, Turkish very often says noun + SUFFIX, or noun + POSTPOSITION — the relationship word sits on the opposite side.

This is exactly why "bahçede" isn't a separate vocabulary word to memorize — it's "bahçe" (garden) plus the locative suffix -de ("in/at"), doing the same job English does with the preposition "in." You'll meet this suffix properly in the upcoming locative-case lesson, and you'll get a whole lesson on postpositions like "önce," "sonra," and "gibi" that work as separate words placed after their noun rather than suffixes glued onto it.

title: The Copula — Basics ("to be")
explanation:
English uses the verb to be (am, is, are) as a separate word. Turkish works differently. In the present tense, there is usually no separate word for "to be". Instead, the meaning of "am", "are", or "is" is added directly to the end of a noun or adjective as a suffix.

This makes Turkish sentences shorter and more compact. Compare these examples:

I am a teacher. → Öğretmenim.

You are happy. → Mutlusun.

She is tired. → Yorgun.

For the singular persons, the copula endings are:

  • -im / -ım / -um / -üm — I am
  • -sin / -sın / -sun / -sün — you are
  • (-dir / -dır / -dur / -dür) — he / she / it is (usually omitted in everyday speech)

Notice that the third person is special. Although Turkish has an optional ending (-dir), native speakers normally leave it out unless they want to sound especially formal, make a definition, or add emphasis.

For example:

  • Doktorum. = I am a doctor.
  • Öğrencisin. = You are a student.
  • Doktor. = He/She is a doctor.
  • Mutlu. = He/She is happy.

The exact form of the suffix follows vowel harmony, so its vowel changes to match the word it attaches to. This may seem like a lot at first, but after seeing a few examples it becomes very predictable.

In the next exercises, you'll practise adding these endings to different nouns and adjectives until forming simple "to be" sentences feels natural.

title: The Copula — Plural & Buffer Letters
explanation:
Now let's look at the plural forms of the Turkish copula. Just like the singular forms, Turkish doesn't use a separate word for to be. Instead, you add an ending directly to the noun or adjective.

The plural endings are:

  • -iz / -ız / -uz / -üz — we are
  • -siniz / -sınız / -sunuz / -sünüz — you are (plural or polite singular)
  • -ler / -lar — they are (used when needed)

Examples:

  • Öğretmeniz. = We are teachers.
  • Mutluyuz. = We are happy.
  • Doktorsunuz. = You are doctors.
  • Yorgunlar. = They are tired.

Notice that the plural endings also follow vowel harmony, so their vowels change to match the word they are attached to.

Buffer letters

If a word already ends in a vowel, Turkish often inserts a buffer letter to avoid two vowels meeting. The most common buffer letter is y.

For example:

  • mutlu + uz → mutluyuz (we are happy)
  • öğrenci + iz → öğrenciyiz (we are students)
  • iyi + iz → iyiyiz (we are well)

Without the buffer letter, these words would be difficult to pronounce. You'll encounter buffer letters throughout Turkish grammar, so getting used to them now will make later lessons much easier.

In the exercises, you'll practise choosing the correct copula ending and adding buffer letters whenever they're needed.

title: The Copula — Questions & Negation
explanation:
Now that you know how to form basic "to be" sentences, it's time to learn how to turn them into questions and negative sentences. Fortunately, both are very regular.

Questions

To ask a yes/no question, Turkish uses the question particle mi / mı / mu / mü. Like many other endings, its vowel changes according to vowel harmony.

Unlike English, the question particle is written as a separate word. It comes before the personal ending.

Examples:

  • Öğretmen misin? = Are you a teacher?
  • Mutlu musunuz? = Are you happy?
  • Hasta mı? = Is he/she ill?

Negation

To say that someone or something is not something, Turkish does not add a negative suffix. Instead, it uses the separate word değil, meaning not. The personal ending is then attached to değil, not to the noun or adjective.

Examples:

  • Öğretmen değilim. = I am not a teacher.
  • Yorgun değilsin. = You are not tired.
  • Doktor değil. = He/She is not a doctor.
  • Hazır değiliz. = We are not ready.

You can also combine questions and negation:

  • Öğretmen değil misin? = Aren't you a teacher?
  • Mutlu değil mi? = Isn't he/she happy?

One final tip: Turkish often leaves out personal pronouns such as ben (I) or sen (you), because the personal endings already make it clear who is being talked about. For example, Öğretmen değilim. already means I am not a teacher without needing the word ben.

In the next exercises, you'll practise making positive, negative, and question sentences until these patterns become automatic.

title: Existence & Possession (var/yok)
explanation:
Turkish doesn't have a verb "to have." Instead, it expresses existence and possession using two special words: var (exists / there is / there are) and yok (doesn't exist / there isn't / there aren't). To say you "have" something, you literally say that the thing "exists at/for you," using a possessive suffix on the noun.

This is a completely different logic from English, so it's worth slowing down on it.

First, the simple existence sense — no possession involved, just "there is/are":

  • Su var. = There is water.
  • Para yok. = There is no money.
  • Zaman var mı? = Is there time?

To turn this into possession ("I have..."), add a possessive suffix to the noun, then follow it with var or yok:

  • param var = I have money (para + m "my" + var = "my money exists")
  • zamanım yok = I don't have time (zaman + ım "my" + yok = "my time doesn't exist")
  • arabası var = he/she has a car (araba + sı "his/her" + var)
  • kitabın var mı? = do you have a book? (kitap + ın "your" + var + mı)

Notice the word order: [thing + possessive suffix] + var/yok. The possessor ("I", "you", "he") never appears as a separate word here — it's built into the possessive suffix on the noun, just like the personal endings you saw in "How Turkish Works," except here they attach to nouns instead of verbs.

The possessive suffixes follow the usual four-way vowel harmony (i/ı/u/ü) and take a buffer letter after vowels, same pattern as elsewhere in Turkish:

  • param = my money (para + m)
  • arkadaşım = my friend (arkadaş + ım)
  • evim = my house (ev + im)
  • arabası = his/her car (araba + sı, buffer -s- after a vowel)

To make a question, add the question particle mı/mi/mu/mü right after var or yok, following normal vowel harmony:

  • Paran var mı? = Do you have money?
  • Zamanınız yok mu? = Don't you (plural/formal) have time?

Full sentence examples pulling this together:

  • Benim bir kedim var. = I have a cat. (the "benim" is optional — the suffix already shows it's "my")
  • Kardeşimin arabası var. = My sibling has a car.
  • Hiç param yok. = I have no money at all.
  • Onun çok arkadaşı var. = He/she has a lot of friends.

A useful mnemonic is the question var mı? = "is there / do you have?" — you'll hear it constantly in shops, cafés, and everyday conversation, always following whatever exists or is being asked about.

In the exercises, you'll practise attaching the right possessive suffix to nouns and choosing var or yok to express existence and possession correctly.

title: Nouns & Plural
explanation:
Turkish nouns are refreshingly simple. Unlike many European languages, they have no grammatical gender, so you never need to remember whether a noun is masculine, feminine, or neuter. There are also no articles, meaning Turkish has no words for a, an, or the. The context tells you which meaning is intended.

For example:

  • Ev büyük. = The house is big. / A house is big.
  • Kitap masada. = The book is on the table.

To make a noun plural, Turkish adds the suffix -ler or -lar. The choice depends on vowel harmony: words with front vowels take -ler, while words with back vowels take -lar.

Examples:

  • ev → evler = house → houses
  • şehir → şehirler = city → cities
  • kitap → kitaplar = book → books
  • araba → arabalar = car → cars

One important rule is that Turkish does not use the plural after numbers. The number already shows that there is more than one, so the noun stays singular.

For example:

  • üç kitap = three books (literally: three book)
  • beş ev = five houses
  • iki öğrenci = two students

You only use -ler/-lar when the noun is plural without a number:

  • Kitaplar masada. = The books are on the table.
  • Öğrenciler geldi. = The students arrived.

In the following exercises, you'll practise choosing the correct plural ending and learn when Turkish uses the plural—and when it doesn't.

title: Simple Adjectives
explanation:
Adjectives describe nouns by giving more information about them, such as their size, colour, age, or quality. Turkish adjectives are very straightforward and much simpler than in many other languages.

Like English, Turkish adjectives come before the noun they describe.

Examples:

  • büyük ev = big house
  • küçük araba = small car
  • güzel şehir = beautiful city
  • iyi arkadaş = good friend

One of the nicest things about Turkish adjectives is that they never change form. They don't agree with the noun in gender or number, because Turkish has neither grammatical gender nor adjective agreement.

For example:

  • büyük ev = big house
  • büyük evler = big houses
  • güzel çocuk = beautiful child
  • güzel çocuklar = beautiful children

Notice that only the noun changes. The adjective stays exactly the same.

Adjectives can also be used on their own to describe something. In these sentences, English uses the verb to be, while Turkish simply places the adjective after the noun.

Examples:

  • Ev büyük. = The house is big.
  • Araba yeni. = The car is new.
  • Kitap ilginç. = The book is interesting.

As you learned in the previous lessons, Turkish normally leaves out the third-person copula, so there is no separate word for is in sentences like these.

In the next exercises, you'll practise using common adjectives both before nouns and as descriptions in simple sentences.

title: The Question Particle
explanation:
One of the easiest ways to ask a yes/no question in Turkish is by using the question particle mi / mı / mu / mü. The form you use depends on vowel harmony.

Unlike most Turkish endings, the question particle is written as a separate word, not attached to the previous word.

Examples:

  • İyi misin? = Are you well?
  • Öğretmen misiniz? = Are you a teacher?
  • Hazır mı? = Is he/she ready?
  • Geldi mi? = Did he/she arrive?

The question particle comes after the word being questioned. If there is a personal ending, it attaches to the question particle instead.

Compare:

  • Mutlusun. = You are happy.
  • Mutlu musun? = Are you happy?

The same pattern works with verbs:

  • Geliyor. = He/She is coming.
  • Geliyor mu? = Is he/she coming?

Remember that mi / mı / mu / mü is almost always written as its own word. This makes it one of the few common grammatical elements in Turkish that isn't attached directly to the word before it.

In the next exercises, you'll practise turning statements into questions and choosing the correct form of the question particle using vowel harmony.

title: Question Words (ne/kim/nerede/ne zaman/nasıl/kaç/hangi/neden)
explanation:
Question words are the small words that let you ask "what," "who," "where," "when," "how," "how many," and "which." In Turkish they don't change the word order much — you usually just drop the question word into the sentence where the answer would go, keeping the verb at the end.

Here are the core question words you need:

  • ne = what
  • kim = who
  • nerede = where
  • ne zaman = when
  • nasıl = how
  • kaç = how many/how much
  • hangi = which
  • neden / niçin / niye = why

Basic examples:

  • Bu ne? = What is this?
  • O kim? = Who is that?
  • Nerede oturuyorsun? = Where do you live?
  • Ne zaman geliyorsun? = When are you coming?
  • Nasılsın? = How are you?
  • Neden geç kaldın? = Why are you late?

A few of these need a little extra care:

1. "Nasıl" and "hangi" behave like adjectives — they sit directly before the noun they describe, with no suffix needed:

  • Nasıl bir ev? = What kind of house?
  • Hangi kitap? = Which book?
  • Hangi gün? = Which day?

2. "Kaç" is followed by a singular noun, just like numbers in Turkish (you already saw this pattern with counting):

  • Kaç kitap? = How many books? (literally "how many book")
  • Kaç yaşındasın? = How old are you? (literally "you are of how many years")

3. "Nerede" changes ending depending on direction, the same way any noun does with locative/dative suffixes: nerede (where, locative) vs. nereye (to where, dative) vs. nereden (from where, ablative):

  • Nerede çalışıyorsun? = Where do you work?
  • Nereye gidiyorsun? = Where are you going?
  • Nereden geliyorsun? = Where are you coming from?

More full-sentence examples:

  • Bu kitap kimin? = Whose book is this?
  • Kaç kardeşin var? = How many siblings do you have?
  • Hangi otobüs Taksim'e gidiyor? = Which bus goes to Taksim?
  • Yemek nasıl? = How is the food?

That "kaç ... var" pattern connects directly to the previous lesson: since var/yok is how Turkish expresses "there is/are," asking about a quantity naturally becomes Kaç ... var? ("How many ... are there?") — for example Evde kaç oda var? = How many rooms are there in the house?

4. "Neden"/"niçin"/"niye" are all "why", interchangeably in most everyday contexts — neden and niçin are the more neutral/written forms, niye is the more casual/spoken one:

  • Neden ağlıyorsun? = Why are you crying?
  • Niye gülüyorsun? = Why are you laughing?

Notice that Turkish question words don't move to the front of the sentence the way English "wh-words" do — they simply replace the piece of information being asked about, wherever it would normally go.

In the exercises, you'll practise choosing the right question word for a given answer and building full questions with the correct word order and suffixes.

title: Negation
explanation:
Turkish has different ways to make a sentence negative, depending on whether you're talking about being something or doing something.

Negating "to be"

For sentences with the copula ("to be"), Turkish uses the separate word değil, meaning not. The personal ending is added to değil, not to the noun or adjective.

Examples:

  • İyi değilim. = I am not well.
  • Öğrenci değilsin. = You are not a student.
  • Öğretmen değil. = He/She is not a teacher.
  • Mutlu değiliz. = We are not happy.

Negating verbs

Verbs work differently. Instead of using değil, Turkish inserts the negative suffix -me- / -ma- directly into the verb, before the tense and personal endings.

For example:

  • Geliyorum. = I am coming.
  • Gelmiyorum. = I am not coming.
  • Konuşuyor. = He/She is speaking.
  • Konuşmuyor. = He/She is not speaking.

You'll learn verb negation in detail in the next lessons. For now, it's enough to remember one simple rule: use değil to negate nouns and adjectives, but use -me-/-ma- to negate verbs.

In the following exercises, you'll practise recognising and forming negative sentences using these two common patterns.

title: Verbs: Present Continuous
explanation:
The Turkish present continuous tense is one of the most important verb forms to learn because it is used constantly in everyday conversations. It is often the first verb tense learners encounter because it covers many situations where English would use either the present continuous (I am doing) or sometimes the simple present (I do).

The main tense marker is -iyor. Because of vowel harmony, it appears in four forms:

  • -iyor
  • -ıyor
  • -uyor
  • -üyor

The ending is added to the verb stem, and then a personal ending shows who is doing the action.

Examples:

  • geliyorum = I am coming / I come
  • gidiyorsun = You are going
  • okuyor = He/She is reading
  • bekliyoruz = We are waiting

Let's break down a word:

geliyorum

  • gel- = come (verb root)
  • -iyor = present continuous
  • -um = I

So geliyorum literally means: come + currently + I → "I am coming."

Turkish often uses this tense more broadly than English. It can describe something happening right now, but also regular situations or things happening around the current period.

Examples:

  • Türkçe öğreniyorum. = I am learning Turkish.
  • Her gün çalışıyorum. = I work/study every day.
  • İstanbul'da yaşıyor. = He/She lives in Istanbul.

The personal endings used after -iyor follow the same general pattern you already learned with the copula. This is one of the helpful features of Turkish: once you understand how endings work, many new grammar structures become combinations of familiar pieces.

In the exercises, you'll practise building present continuous verbs by combining the verb root, the -iyor tense marker, and the correct personal ending.

title: Simple Sentences (SOV)
explanation:
Now it's time to combine the pieces you have learned and build complete Turkish sentences. The most important thing to remember is Turkish word order: Subject – Object – Verb (SOV).

Unlike English, where the verb usually comes before the object, Turkish places the action at the end of the sentence.

Compare:

English: The cat drinks milk.

Turkish: Kedi süt içer.

Literally:

Cat milk drinks.

This may feel unusual at first, but the pattern is very consistent. Once you know that the verb comes last, longer sentences become much easier to understand.

More examples:

  • Ben kitap okuyorum. = I am reading a book.
  • Ali kahve içiyor. = Ali is drinking coffee.
  • Çocuk top oynuyor. = The child is playing with a ball.

Turkish also has different verb tenses that give slightly different meanings. The sentence Kedi süt içer. uses the aorist tense, which describes general truths, habits, repeated actions, or things that usually happen.

Compare these two sentences:

  • Kedi süt içer. = The cat drinks milk. (a general habit or fact)
  • Kedi süt içiyor. = The cat is drinking milk. (happening right now)

Both can translate into English using the present tense, but Turkish makes a clear distinction between a regular action and an action happening at this moment.

Another important feature is that Turkish often drops the subject pronoun when it is already clear from the verb ending.

For example:

  • Kitap okuyorum. = I am reading a book.
  • Türkçe öğreniyoruz. = We are learning Turkish.

The words ben (I) and biz (we) are not necessary because the verb ending already tells us who is acting.

In the exercises, you'll practise recognising the SOV pattern, placing words in the correct order, and building your first complete Turkish sentences.

title: Possessive Suffixes
explanation:
Turkish expresses ownership in a very different way from English. Instead of putting a separate word like my, your, or their before the noun, Turkish usually adds a possessive suffix directly to the end of the noun.

Think of the noun as carrying the information about who owns it.

For example:

  • ev = house
  • evim = my house
  • evin = your house
  • evi = his/her/its house
  • evimiz = our house
  • eviniz = your house (plural or formal)
  • evleri = their house

Let's break one word down:

evimiz

  • ev = house
  • -imiz = our

So the meaning is built directly into the word: house + our → "our house".

The possessive suffixes change according to vowel harmony, just like the other suffixes you have already learned.

Examples:

  • kitap → kitabım = my book
  • araba → arabamız = our car
  • göz → gözüm = my eye

You may notice that some words change slightly when a suffix is added. For example, kitap becomes kitabım. This is a common sound change in Turkish where certain final consonants soften before vowel-starting suffixes.

Turkish can also use a separate possessive pronoun for extra emphasis, but the possessive suffix on the noun is still required.

Compare:

  • Evim. = My house.
  • Benim evim. = My house. (emphasising that it belongs to me)

In the second sentence, benim means "my", but evim still contains the possessive ending. Turkish does not say just benim ev; the noun must still show ownership.

In the exercises, you'll practise recognising and building possessive forms until these suffixes become as natural as the English words "my", "your", and "their".

title: Demonstrative Pronouns (bu/şu/o)
explanation:
Demonstrative pronouns point to specific things based on how close they are to the speaker or listener. English mostly squeezes this into a two-way system — "this" versus "that" — but Turkish uses a three-way system: bu, şu, and o.

These words can stand alone as pronouns ("this one") or sit directly in front of a noun as adjectives ("this book") — unlike suffixes you've seen before, they are separate words and never attach to the noun.

The three forms:

  • bu = this (near the speaker)
  • şu = that (near the listener, or something you're pointing out close by)
  • o = that (far from both speaker and listener — also the word for "he/she/it")

Basic examples:

  • bu kitap = this book (in my hand or right next to me)
  • şu adam = that man (near you, or nearby and pointed at)
  • o ev = that house (over there, away from us both)
  • bu araba = this car
  • o çocuk = that child

The tricky part is şu — English has no separate word for it, so it often gets translated as "that" too. Think of şu as "that one right there, close to you" or as a way to draw attention to something, often with a pointing gesture, as opposed to o, which refers to something more distant or already known.

  • Bu ne? = What is this? (something near me)
  • Şu ne? = What is that? (something near you / nearby I'm pointing at)
  • O ne? = What is that? (something far away)

When used alone as pronouns (standing in for a noun rather than describing one), these words can take case suffixes just like nouns, with a small twist: bu and şu double their consonant before a vowel suffix.

  • bu + a → buna = to this
  • şu + a → şuna = to that
  • o + a → ona = to that/him/her (no doubling — o is irregular here)

Full sentence examples:

  • Bu ev büyük. = This house is big.
  • Şu araba senin mi? = Is that car yours?
  • O kadın öğretmen. = That woman is a teacher.
  • Bunu istiyorum. = I want this (one).
  • Şunu görüyor musun? = Do you see that (one)?

Compare this with the question word hangi ("which") from the previous lesson: hangi kitap? asks "which book?", and bu kitap, şu kitap, or o kitap can all serve as the answer, depending on how close the book is.

A handy way to remember the three-way split: bu is in your hand, şu is in your friend's hand or right there when you point, and o is across the room or out of sight.

In the exercises, you'll practise choosing the right demonstrative based on distance, using them both before nouns and as standalone pronouns.

title: Case: Accusative
explanation:
Turkish uses case suffixes to show the role a noun plays in a sentence. The accusative case is used when a noun is the specific, definite direct object of a verb — the thing that is directly affected by the action.

The accusative suffix has four forms because of vowel harmony:

  • -i
  • -ı
  • -u
  • -ü

The main idea is this: if you are talking about a particular thing that the listener can identify, the noun usually receives the accusative suffix.

Compare these two sentences:

  • Elma yedim. = I ate an apple. / I ate apples. (not a specific apple)
  • Elmayı yedim. = I ate the apple. (a specific apple that we both know about)

The English translation often uses a versus the, but Turkish marks this difference directly on the noun.

More examples:

  • Kitap okuyorum. = I am reading a book / books.
  • Kitabı okuyorum. = I am reading the book.
  • Filmi izledim. = I watched the movie.
  • Arabayı gördüm. = I saw the car.

Notice the structure:

noun + accusative suffix + verb

For example:

kitap + ı + okuyorum → kitabı okuyorum

The accusative suffix can also cause small sound changes in some words. For example, words ending in p, ç, t, k may soften when a vowel-starting suffix is added:

  • kitap → kitabı = the book (object)
  • ağaç → ağacı = the tree (object)

This is another example of Turkish keeping pronunciation smooth when adding suffixes.

In the exercises, you'll practise deciding whether an object is general or specific and adding the correct accusative ending when needed.

title: Case: Locative
explanation:
The locative case is used to show where something or someone is located. It often replaces the English prepositions at, in, and on.

Instead of using a separate word before the noun, Turkish adds a location suffix directly to the end of the noun.

The locative suffix has four possible forms because of vowel harmony:

  • -de
  • -da
  • -te
  • -ta

The choice depends on the final vowel and final consonant of the word.

Basic examples:

  • evde = at home / in the house
  • okulda = at school
  • masada = on the table
  • parkta = in the park

Let's look at how these words are built:

  • ev + de → evde = house + at/in → at home
  • okul + da → okulda = school + at → at school
  • masa + da → masada = table + on → on the table

Examples in full sentences:

  • Ben evdeyim. = I am at home.
  • Çocuk okulda. = The child is at school.
  • Kitap masada. = The book is on the table.
  • Ali parkta oynuyor. = Ali is playing in the park.

Notice that Turkish does not need separate words like in, at, or on. The location information is built into the noun itself.

A useful thing to remember is that the locative answers the question:

Nerede? = Where?

For example:

  • Nerede? — Where?
  • Evde. — At home.
  • Okulda. — At school.

In the exercises, you'll practise recognising locations and choosing the correct locative ending based on vowel harmony and pronunciation rules.

title: Case: Dative
explanation:
The dative case shows movement or direction towards something, or the indirect object of an action ("to/for someone/something"). It replaces the English preposition to (and often for, when someone is receiving something).

Like the locative you just learned, the dative isn't a separate word — it's a suffix glued directly onto the noun.

The dative suffix has two main forms, following two-way vowel harmony:

  • -e (after front vowels: e, i, ö, ü)
  • -a (after back vowels: a, ı, o, u)

Basic examples:

  • eve = to home / homeward
  • okula = to school
  • Ankara'ya = to Ankara
  • kitaba = to the book / for the book

Two extra rules make dative forms slightly trickier than the locative:

1. A buffer "-y-" appears if the word already ends in a vowel (Turkish never allows two vowels to collide):

  • araba + a → arabaya = car + to → to the car
  • kapı + a → kapıya = door + to → to the door
  • Ali + e → Ali'ye = Ali + to → to Ali (apostrophe before the suffix on proper names)

2. Some words "soften" their final consonant (a rule called ünsüz yumuşaması) when a suffix starting with a vowel is added: p→b, ç→c, t→d, k→ğ.

  • kitap + a → kitaba = book + to → to the book (p → b)
  • ağaç + a → ağaca = tree + to → to the tree (ç → c)
  • dolap + a → dolaba = cupboard + to → to the cupboard (p → b)

You'll see this same softening pattern again in later suffixes — it's not unique to the dative, so it's worth getting used to now.

Examples in full sentences:

  • Eve gidiyorum. = I am going home.
  • Okula gidiyor. = He/she is going to school.
  • Ona kitap verdim. = I gave a book to him/her.
  • Anneme bakıyorum. = I am looking at my mother. (bakmak "to look" always takes a dative object in Turkish, even though English uses "at")

That last example matters: several common Turkish verbs pair with the dative even where the English translation doesn't use "to" — bakmak (to look at), başlamak (to start [something]), inanmak (to believe in), binmek (to get on/board). You'll meet more of these as you go; for now, just notice that "to" in English doesn't always predict the dative, and vice versa.

Compare with the locative from the previous lesson: same root, one different vowel/letter in the suffix, completely different meaning — evde (at home, locative) vs. eve (to home, dative). This is agglutination doing real work for you.

A useful mnemonic is the question the dative answers:

Nereye? = (To) where? / Kime? = To whom?

  • Nereye gidiyorsun? — Where are you going?
  • Okula. — To school.

In the exercises, you'll practise building the correct dative form (including the buffer -y- and consonant softening where relevant) and recognising when a verb requires a dative object.

title: Case: Ablative
explanation:
The ablative case shows movement away from something, or the origin/source of something. It replaces the English preposition from (and sometimes "out of" or "than," depending on context).

Just like the locative and dative you've already seen, the ablative isn't a separate word — it's a suffix attached directly onto the noun.

The ablative suffix has two main forms, following two-way vowel harmony (and it also changes voicing depending on the preceding sound):

  • -den (after front vowels: e, i, ö, ü)
  • -dan (after back vowels: a, ı, o, u)
  • -ten / -tan (after unvoiced consonants: ç, f, h, k, p, s, ş, t)

Basic examples:

  • okuldan = from school
  • evden = from home
  • Ankara'dan = from Ankara
  • parktan = from the park
  • kitaptan = from the book

Notice the last two: because park and kitap end in unvoiced consonants (k, p), the suffix uses its unvoiced form -tan/-ten instead of -dan/-den. This is the same kind of sound-matching you saw with vowel harmony, just applied to consonants.

Unlike the dative, the ablative never needs a buffer letter for vowel-final words, since d/t can follow a vowel directly:

  • araba + dan → arabadan = car + from → from the car
  • kapı + dan → kapıdan = door + from → from the door

Examples in full sentences:

  • Okuldan geldim. = I came from school.
  • Evden çıkıyorum. = I am leaving (from) the house.
  • Ondan bir mektup aldım. = I received a letter from him/her.
  • Bu kitaptan çok şey öğrendim. = I learned a lot from this book.
  • Türkiye'den geliyorum. = I am coming from Turkey.

Some common verbs pair naturally with the ablative even where English phrasing might not obviously suggest "from" — korkmak (to be afraid of), hoşlanmak (to like/be fond of), bahsetmek (to talk about). For example: köpekten korkuyorum = I am afraid of the dog (literally "from the dog"). Keep an eye out for these as you progress.

A useful mnemonic is the question the ablative answers:

Nereden? = From where? / Kimden? = From whom?

  • Nereden geliyorsun? — Where are you coming from?
  • Okuldan. — From school.

In the exercises, you'll practise building correct ablative forms (including the unvoiced -ten/-tan variant) and using them in sentences that express origin or movement away from something.

title: Past Tense
explanation:
The definite past tense describes actions that happened and that you witnessed or are certain about — it's the everyday equivalent of English "-ed" (came, went, saw, did). In Turkish, this meaning is carried entirely by a suffix attached straight onto the verb stem.

The past tense suffix is -di, and like other suffixes it follows vowel harmony — but this one has four vowel variants instead of two, plus a voiceless-consonant twist:

  • -dı (after a, ı)
  • -di (after e, i)
  • -du (after o, u)
  • -dü (after ö, ü)

Basic examples with personal endings attached:

  • geldim = I came (gel + di + m)
  • baktım = I looked (bak + tı + m)
  • gördüm = I saw (gör + dü + m)
  • okudum = I read (oku + du + m)

1. Voiceless assimilation: if the verb stem ends in one of the voiceless consonants ç, f, h, k, p, s, ş, t, the suffix's "d" turns into "t":

  • git + ti → gitti = went (not "gitdi")
  • bak + tı → baktı = he/she looked
  • iç + ti → içti = he/she drank

This is the same kind of consonant behavior you saw with softening in the dative case, just working in the opposite direction: there, a suffix made a hard consonant softer; here, a suffix itself hardens to match the stem.

The full personal endings for the past tense are: -m, -n, (none), -k, -niz, -ler (with the usual vowel-harmony matching), giving a full pattern like:

  • geldim = I came
  • geldin = you came
  • geldi = he/she/it came
  • geldik = we came
  • geldiniz = you (pl./formal) came
  • geldiler = they came

Examples in full sentences:

  • Dün eve geldim. = I came home yesterday.
  • Okula gittin mi? = Did you go to school?
  • Kitabı okudu. = He/she read the book.
  • Onu görmedik. = We didn't see him/her. (negative -me/-ma before the past suffix)

Turkish actually has a second past tense, marked with -miş, used for things you heard about or inferred rather than witnessed directly — a distinction English doesn't make. That's a topic for a later lesson once this witnessed past feels natural.

A useful mnemonic is the question this tense answers:

Ne zaman? = When? / Ne yaptın? = What did you do?

  • Ne yaptın? — What did you do?
  • Eve geldim. — I came home.

In the exercises, you'll practise attaching the correct vowel-harmony and voiceless-consonant form of the past suffix and building full past-tense sentences.

title: The Infinitive
explanation:
The infinitive is the basic, unconjugated "dictionary form" of a verb — like English "to go" or "to eat." In Turkish, it's made by adding a suffix directly to the verb stem, and every verb you look up in a dictionary appears in this form.

The infinitive suffix has two forms, following two-way vowel harmony:

  • -mek (after front vowels: e, i, ö, ü)
  • -mak (after back vowels: a, ı, o, u)

Basic examples:

  • git + mek → gitmek = to go
  • ye + mek → yemek = to eat
  • gel + mek → gelmek = to come
  • oku + mak → okumak = to read
  • bak + mak → bakmak = to look

On its own, the infinitive is what a verb looks like before you conjugate it for tense and person (compare gitmek "to go" with gidiyorum "I am going," from the tenses you've already studied). But its most common everyday use is pairing with another verb, much like English "want to," "need to," or "have to":

  • gitmek istiyorum = I want to go
  • okumak istiyor = he/she wants to read
  • gelmek gerekiyor = it's necessary to come / I need to come

The verb istemek (to want) is the one you'll meet constantly: just take any infinitive and add a conjugated form of istemek after it.

  • Yemek yemek istiyorum. = I want to eat food. (yes, "yemek" appears twice here — once as the noun "food/meal," once as the infinitive "to eat")
  • Eve gitmek istiyorum. = I want to go home.
  • Türkçe konuşmak istiyor musun? = Do you want to speak Turkish?

Another very common pairing is gerekmek (to be necessary), which expresses "must/need to":

  • Çalışmak gerekiyor. = It's necessary to work. / I have to work.

Unlike the past tense you just learned, where the verb changes to show who did the action and when, the infinitive itself never changes — it stays exactly the same (-mek/-mak) no matter who "wants" or "needs" to do it. All the conjugation happens on the helper verb (istemek, gerekmek) that follows it.

In the exercises, you'll practise forming infinitives with correct vowel harmony and combining them with istemek and gerekmek to express wants and needs.

title: Numbers & Ordinals
explanation:
Turkish cardinal numbers (bir, iki, üç... "one, two, three...") are simple, fixed words with no conjugation. Ordinal numbers ("first, second, third...") are built from them by adding a suffix, similar to how English adds "-th" (with irregulars like "first, second, third").

The ordinal suffix is -(i)ncı / -(i)nci / -(i)uncu / -(i)üncü, following four-way vowel harmony (and matching the buffer vowel to the last vowel of the root):

  • -inci (after e, i)
  • -ıncı (after a, ı)
  • -üncü (after ö, ü)
  • -uncu (after o, u)

Basic examples:

  • bir (one) → birinci (first)
  • iki (two) → ikinci (second)
  • üç (three) → üçüncü (third)
  • dört (four) → dördüncü (fourth)
  • on (ten) → onuncu (tenth)

A couple of small irregularities to notice:

1. "dört" softens its final consonant when the suffix is added (t → d), just like the consonant softening you've seen elsewhere:

  • dört + üncü → dördüncü = four + th → fourth

2. "altı" (six) drops its final vowel before the suffix, to avoid two vowels in a row:

  • altı + ıncı → altıncı = six + th → sixth

Examples in full sentences:

  • Bu benim ilk kez. = This is my first time. (ilk is an irregular alternative to "birinci" for "first")
  • Üçüncü kattayım. = I am on the third floor.
  • Bu yılın ikinci ayı. = It's the second month of the year.
  • Onuncu sınıftayım. = I am in tenth grade.

Remember from the noun lesson: numbers keep the following noun singular, not plural — üç kitap (three books), not "üç kitaplar". The same holds with ordinals: üçüncü kitap (the third book).

Unlike the infinitive you just learned, which is a verb form built with -mek/-mak, ordinals are built directly onto number roots with their own harmonizing suffix — but the underlying idea is the same: Turkish prefers to build precise meaning by stacking suffixes onto a stable root rather than using separate words.

A useful mnemonic is the question word Kaçıncı? = "Which one (in order)? / What number?":

  • Kaçıncı kattasın? — Which floor are you on?
  • Üçüncü katta. — On the third floor.

In the exercises, you'll practise turning cardinal numbers into their ordinal forms and using them correctly with singular nouns.

title: The Imperative
explanation:
The imperative is the command form of a verb — used to tell someone to do (or not do) something. In English this is just the bare verb ("Come!", "Sit!"), but Turkish marks who you're commanding with different endings, since it distinguishes informal sen (you, singular) from formal/plural siz (you, plural or polite).

To form the informal command, just take the bare verb stem — no suffix needed at all:

  • gel- → Gel! = Come!
  • otur- → Otur! = Sit!
  • bak- → Bak! = Look!
  • yaz- → Yaz! = Write!

For the formal/plural command, add -in/-ın/-un/-ün (four-way vowel harmony) to the stem:

  • gel + in → Gelin! = Come! (siz)
  • otur + un → Oturun! = Sit! (siz)
  • bak + ın → Bakın! = Look! (siz)
  • yaz + ın → Yazın! = Write! (siz)

This same siz form is also used simply to be polite with one person you don't know well, even if you're not addressing a group — much like vous in French.

Negative commands are made by inserting -me/-ma right after the stem, before any ending — this is the same negative suffix you'll see attached to other verb tenses too:

  • gel + me → Gelme! = Don't come!
  • bak + ma → Bakma! = Don't look!
  • gel + me + yin → Gelmeyin! = Don't come! (siz)
  • bak + ma + yın → Bakmayın! = Don't look! (siz)

Notice that in the negative siz form, a buffer -y- appears between -me/-ma and the -in/-ın ending, since two vowels would otherwise collide.

Examples in full context:

  • Kapıyı aç! = Open the door!
  • Buraya gelin! = Come here! (siz)
  • Korkma! = Don't be afraid!
  • Endişelenmeyin. = Don't worry. (siz)

The imperative is one of the most common verb forms you'll hear in everyday spoken Turkish — on signs, in instructions, and in casual requests among friends and family, so it's worth recognizing instantly even before you've mastered other tenses.

In the exercises, you'll practise building both the sen and siz command forms, along with their negative versions.

title: Past Copula
explanation:
You already know that Turkish attaches "to be" directly onto nouns and adjectives as a suffix rather than using a separate word, like öğrenciyim (I am a student). The past copula works the same way, but pushes the meaning into the past: "was/were". It replaces English sentences like "I was a student" or "He was sick" — no separate verb needed, just another suffix.

The past copula suffix is -ydi, with four vowel-harmony variants:

  • -ydı (after a, ı)
  • -ydi (after e, i)
  • -ydu (after o, u)
  • -ydü (after ö, ü)

Basic examples:

  • öğrenciydim = I was a student
  • hastaydı = he/she was sick
  • yorgunduk = we were tired
  • mutluydunuz = you (plural/formal) were happy

Notice that the "y" in "-ydi" is a buffer consonant, just like the buffer -y- you saw with the dative case — it appears because the word already ends in a vowel and Turkish avoids two vowels colliding. After a consonant, the suffix simply starts with the vowel, no buffer needed: hasta + ydı → hastaydı, but yorgun + du → yorgundu → yorgunduk (no y, since "yorgun" ends in a consonant).

The past copula attaches to the same personal-ending set you already learned for the present copula, just with -ydi- inserted before those endings:

  • öğrenci + ydi + m → öğrenciydim = I was a student
  • hasta + ydı + n → hastaydın = you were sick
  • yorgun + du + k → yorgunduk = we were tired

Full sentence examples:

  • Ben öğrenciydim. = I was a student.
  • O hastaydı. = He/she was sick.
  • Biz yorgunduk. = We were tired.
  • Siz mutluydunuz. = You were happy.
  • Onlar öğretmendi. = They were teachers. (the 3rd person plural often drops the extra plural marker in this construction)

Unlike the imperative you just learned, which changes the verb stem itself to give a command, the past copula doesn't touch a verb at all — it turns a noun or adjective into a complete "was/were" statement all by itself.

In the exercises, you'll practise attaching the correct vowel-harmony form of the past copula (with the buffer -y- where needed) and matching it to the right personal ending.

title: Ability: "Can" — Present (-ebiliyor)
explanation:
This chapter focuses only on the Present (-ebiliyor) form of this construction. The other tenses are covered in their own separate chapters, so the exercises here won't mix them in.

Turkish builds "can"/"to be able to" as a SUFFIX inside the verb (-ebil-/-abil-, 2-way harmony), not a separate word. This lesson covers it combined with the present continuous tense (-iyor), used for an ability you are exercising or managing right now, in this period:

  • Bugün erken kalkabiliyorum. = I'm managing to get up early these days.
  • Artık yüzebiliyorum. = I can swim now (a newly gained ability).
  • Türkçe konuşabiliyor musun? = Are you managing to speak Turkish (these days)?

Note that whichever root you start from, once you add -ebil-/-abil-, every suffix that follows takes its FRONT-vowel form — because -ebil-/-abil- itself always ends in a front "i" (from "bil"). So even a back-vowel root like yap- takes the front form -iyor, not "-ıyor":

  • yapabiliyorum = I'm managing to do it (yap + abil + iyor + um — front -iyor, despite the back root)

In the exercises, you'll practise the ability suffix combined specifically with the present continuous tense.

title: Ability: "Can" — General (-ebilir)
explanation:
This chapter focuses only on the General (-ebilir) form of this construction. The other tenses are covered in their own separate chapters, so the exercises here won't mix them in.

Turkish builds "can"/"to be able to" as a SUFFIX inside the verb (-ebil-/-abil-, 2-way harmony), not a separate word. This lesson covers its most common, neutral, everyday form: combined with the aorist tense (-ir), the default way to say a plain "can":

  • gidebilirim = I can go (git + ebil + ir + im)
  • yüzebilirim = I can swim
