  • yapabilirim = I can do it — note the aorist stays -ir here too, not "-ır", even after the back-vowel root yap-, because -ebil-/-abil- itself always ends in a front "i"

Questions add the particle mi/mı/mu/mü separately: Yüzebilir misin? = Can you swim?

The negative ("can't") is irregular — it doesn't add "değil" or the normal "-me-", but replaces -ebil-/-abil- entirely with a short form -eme-/-ama- (which, unlike the positive, DOES follow the root's own 2-way harmony):

  • gidemem = I can't go (the aorist "-ir" drops before "-m"; compare gidemez = he can't go, which keeps it)
  • yapamam = I can't do it (back root → -ama-)

In the exercises, you'll practise both the positive general-ability form and its irregular negative.

title: Ability: "Can" — Past (-ebildi)
explanation:
This chapter focuses only on the Past (-ebildi) form of this construction. The other tenses are covered in their own separate chapters, so the exercises here won't mix them in.

Turkish builds "can"/"to be able to" as a SUFFIX inside the verb (-ebil-/-abil-, 2-way harmony), not a separate word. This lesson covers it combined with the -di past, meaning "was able to (and did)" — a completed, successful attempt, not just theoretical capability:

  • Sonunda gelebildim. = I finally managed to come.
  • Sınavı geçebildi mi? = Did he manage to pass the exam?
  • Yapabildim. = I managed to do it (yap + abil + di + m — front "-di", not "-dı", despite the back root)

The negative uses the irregular short form -eme-/-ama- (root-harmony sensitive) plus the -di past:

  • Gelemedim. = I couldn't come / wasn't able to come.
  • Yapamadı. = He couldn't do it.

In the exercises, you'll practise the ability suffix combined specifically with the -di past, positive and negative.

title: Ability: "Can" — Future (-ebilecek)
explanation:
This chapter focuses only on the Future (-ebilecek) form of this construction. The other tenses are covered in their own separate chapters, so the exercises here won't mix them in.

Turkish builds "can"/"to be able to" as a SUFFIX inside the verb (-ebil-/-abil-, 2-way harmony), not a separate word. This lesson covers it combined with the future tense (-ecek), meaning "will be able to":

  • Yarın gelebileceğim. = I'll be able to come tomorrow. (-ecek + im → -eceğim, the usual k→ğ softening before a vowel)
  • Bunu yapabilecek misin? = Will you be able to do this?
  • yapabilecek = will be able to do it — the future stays -ecek, not "-acak", even after the back-vowel root yap-, because -ebil-/-abil- always ends in a front "i"

The negative uses the irregular short form -eme-/-ama- plus the future:

  • Yarın gelemeyeceğim. = I won't be able to come tomorrow.

In the exercises, you'll practise the ability suffix combined specifically with the future tense, positive and negative.

title: Ability: "Can" — Questions (mi/mı/mu/mü)
explanation:
This chapter focuses only on yes/no questions with this construction. Statement forms are covered in their own separate chapters, so the exercises here focus on the question pattern itself.

To ask a yes/no question with the ability suffix (-ebil-/-abil-), add the question particle mi/mı/mu/mü as a SEPARATE word right after the verb, with the personal ending moving onto the question particle itself:

  • Yüzebilir misin? = Can you swim? (present/general)
  • Yardım edebilir misiniz? = Can you (formal/plural) help?
  • Dün gelebildin mi? = Were you able to come yesterday? (past)
  • Yarın gelebilecek misin? = Will you be able to come tomorrow? (future)

Negative questions ("can't you...?") combine the irregular negative -eme-/-ama- with the question particle:

  • Yüzemez misin? = Can't you swim?
  • Neden gelemedin? = Why couldn't you come? (a wh-question needs no "mi," since the question word itself does the job)

In the exercises, you'll practise turning ability statements into yes/no questions across different tenses.

title: Address Forms & Politeness
explanation:
Turkish has some distinctive habits for addressing people politely that don't map neatly onto English "Mr./Mrs." or "you". Getting these right makes a big difference in how natural (and respectful) you sound.

1. Titles after the first name. Instead of "Mr. Smith" (surname-based), Turkish typically attaches a title to the first name: Bey for men, Hanım for women.

  • Ahmet Bey = Mr. Ahmet
  • Ayşe Hanım = Ms./Mrs. Ayşe
  • Ahmet Bey, nasılsınız? = Mr. Ahmet, how are you?

This is the everyday polite way to address a boss, teacher, shopkeeper, or anyone you don't know well — using a bare surname the English way is rare and can sound cold or bureaucratic.

2. Affectionate/vocative endings. Turkish can soften a term of address by adding a diminutive/affectionate suffix, roughly like adding "dear" or a cutesy tone in English. A common one is -cığım / -ciğim (with its usual vowel-harmony and consonant variants: -cığım, -ciğim, -cuğum, -cüğüm), meaning "my dear ___":

  • anne + ciğim → anneciğim = mommy / my dear mother
  • baba + cığım → babacığım = daddy / my dear father
  • can + ım → canım = dear/darling (extremely common, used with friends, family, even strangers warmly)

You'll hear canım constantly in casual speech — it can mean "honey", "dear", or even just fill in as a friendly way to soften a sentence.

3. Register: sen vs. siz. You've already met sen (informal "you") and siz (formal or plural "you"). The key thing to remember here is that siz always takes the same verb ending as a plural subject, even when you're formally addressing just one person:

  • Nasılsın? = How are you? (informal, one person)
  • Nasılsınız? = How are you? (formal, one person — or informal/formal, multiple people)

Choosing siz plus a title like Bey/Hanım together signals real politeness — for example, with an elder, a stranger, or someone in a professional setting: Ayşe Hanım, yardım edebilir misiniz? = Ms. Ayşe, could you help? (Notice the verb ending -misiniz, matching siz.)

Some more full examples to compare registers and address forms:

  • Ahmet Bey, teşekkür ederim. = Mr. Ahmet, thank you.
  • Anneciğim, neredesin? = Mommy, where are you?
  • Canım, gel buraya. = Honey, come here.
  • Siz nerelisiniz? = Where are you from? (formal)

This connects to the ability suffix -ebilir/-abilir you just learned: polite requests very often combine it with siz, as in yardım edebilir misiniz? (could you help?) — the formal "can you...?" question is one of the most common polite requests you'll make in Turkish.

In the exercises, you'll practise choosing the right title, affectionate ending, and sen/siz register for a given situation, along with matching the verb ending correctly to siz.

title: Noun Compounds
explanation:
Turkish links two nouns together to make compounds like "car key" or "school garden" — but unlike English, it marks this link with suffixes rather than just placing the words side by side. There are two distinct patterns, and telling them apart matters for meaning.

1. Indefinite (belirtisiz) compounds describe a general category or type, not a specific owner. Only the second noun gets a suffix — the possessive -(s)I (following four-way vowel harmony: ı/i/u/ü, with a buffer -s- if the noun ends in a vowel):

  • araba anahtarı = car key (a key of the "car" type, not one particular car's key)
  • elma suyu = apple juice (elma + su + yu, buffer -y-)
  • çay bardağı = tea glass (a glass for tea; ğ appears via the same softening you've seen before)
  • ders kitabı = textbook (literally "lesson book"; kitap softens p→b before the suffix)

2. Definite (belirtili) compounds describe one specific noun's specific possession — "the school's garden," not "a garden of the school type." Here both nouns take suffixes: the first noun gets the genitive -(n)In, and the second gets the same possessive -(s)I as before:

  • okulun bahçesi = the school's garden (okul + un [genitive] + bahçe + si [possessive])
  • çocuğun kitabı = the child's book (çocuk + un, with k→ğ softening; kitap + ı, with p→b softening)
  • Ali'nin arabası = Ali's car (proper names take an apostrophe before both suffixes, as with other cases)

Comparing the two side by side shows how the missing genitive suffix changes the meaning entirely:

  • araba anahtarı = a car key (any car)
  • arabanın anahtarı = the car's key (one particular car)

Examples in full sentences:

  • Araba anahtarını gördün mü? = Did you see the car key?
  • Okulun bahçesi çok büyük. = The school's garden is very big.
  • Çocuğun kitabı masada. = The child's book is on the table.
  • Elma suyu içiyorum. = I'm drinking apple juice.

Unlike the address forms and politeness patterns from the last lesson, which are about choosing the right words for a social situation, this is a structural rule: the suffixes themselves tell you whether a compound is a general category or one specific thing, regardless of context or tone.

Recognising which pattern you're looking at just takes exposure — a quick check is whether the first noun could take "the" and be replaced by "whose": if you can ask Kimin? (whose?) or Neyin? (of what?) and get a clear specific answer, you likely need the full genitive + possessive pair; if it's just naming a type, the indefinite compound is enough.

In the exercises, you'll practise building both compound types correctly and choosing the right one based on whether a specific owner is involved.

title: Postpositions — "için" — purpose
explanation:
This chapter focuses only on the "için" — purpose form/function. The other senses of "için," and the other postpositions, are covered in their own separate chapters, so the exercises here won't mix them in.

için expresses purpose — what something is for, or what goal an action serves. Like all Turkish postpositions, it comes AFTER the noun it governs.

With a plain noun, için stays bare — no case suffix needed:

  • Bu makas kağıt kesmek için. = These scissors are for cutting paper.
  • Bu para tatil için. = This money is for a vacation.

To say "in order to do something," attach için to a verb's infinitive (-mek/-mak):

  • Sınavı geçmek için çok çalıştım. = I studied hard (in order) to pass the exam.
  • Türkçe öğrenmek için buradayım. = I'm here (in order) to learn Turkish.

With a personal pronoun instead of a noun, için takes the GENITIVE — a fixed quirk of this one postposition, not a general rule:

  • Bunu ne için yaptın? = What did you do this for? (purpose, with question word "ne")
  • Onun için buradayım. = I'm here for that (purpose).

In the exercises, you'll practise için expressing purpose/goal — with plain nouns, with the -mek/-mak infinitive, and with personal pronouns.

title: Postpositions — "için" — reason
explanation:
This chapter focuses only on the "için" — reason form/function. The other senses of "için," and the other postpositions, are covered in their own separate chapters, so the exercises here won't mix them in.

Here için expresses a reason or cause — "because of X." Like all Turkish postpositions, it comes AFTER the noun it governs.

With a plain noun, için stays bare — no case suffix needed:

  • Trafik için işe geç kaldım. = I was late for work because of traffic.
  • Bu haber için çok üzüldüm. = I was very upset because of this news.

To give a reason built from an action rather than a bare noun, combine için with a verbal noun (-mek/-mak, or -diği/-eceği + possessive for a specific, already-known event):

  • Geç kaldığım için özür dilerim. = I'm sorry for being late (lit. because of my having been late).
  • Hasta olduğu için gelmedi. = He/she didn't come because he/she was sick.

With a personal pronoun instead of a noun, için takes the GENITIVE — a fixed quirk of this one postposition, not a general rule:

  • Senin için endişelendim. = I worried because of you.

In the exercises, you'll practise için expressing reason/cause — with plain nouns, with the -diği için clause pattern, and with personal pronouns.

title: Postpositions — "için" — benefit
explanation:
This chapter focuses only on the "için" — benefit form/function. The other senses of "için," and the other postpositions, are covered in their own separate chapters, so the exercises here won't mix them in.

Here için expresses benefit or sake — "for X's benefit," "on X's behalf." This is the sense you'll use most often with personal pronouns. Like all Turkish postpositions, it comes AFTER the noun it governs.

With a plain noun, için stays bare — no case suffix needed:

  • Ailem için çalışıyorum. = I work for my family (for their benefit).
  • Bunu senin iyiliğin için söylüyorum. = I'm saying this for your own good.

With a personal pronoun instead of a noun, için takes the GENITIVE — a fixed quirk of this one postposition, not a general rule:

  • Senin için bir hediye aldım. = I bought a gift for you.
  • Benim için önemli değil. = It's not important to/for me.
  • Onun için endişelenme. = Don't worry for his/her sake.

In the exercises, you'll practise için expressing benefit/sake — mostly with personal pronouns (genitive + için), and with a few plain nouns too.

title: Postpositions — "ile" — with
explanation:
This chapter focuses only on "ile." The other postpositions are covered in their own separate chapters, so the exercises here won't mix them in.

ile means "with" (accompaniment or instrument) or "and" (linking two nouns). It very commonly attaches directly to the preceding noun as the suffix -(y)le/-(y)la (2-way harmony, buffer -y- after a vowel) — this attached form is far more common in speech than writing "ile" as a separate word:

  • arkadaşımla geldim / arkadaşım ile geldim = I came with my friend
  • kalemle yazdım = I wrote with a pen
  • çayla kahve = tea and coffee

With a personal pronoun, the singular pronouns fuse in a genitive-flavored way — benimle (with me), seninle (with you), onunla (with him/her) — while the plural ones don't: bizimle (with us), sizinle (with you-pl.), but onlarla (with them, no extra "-in-").

In a list of more than two items, don't chain "ile" — use "ve" instead before the last item: Ece, Su ve Yasemin (NOT "Ece, Su ile Yasemin").

In the exercises, you'll practise "ile," both as a separate word and as the attached -(y)le/-(y)la suffix.

title: Postpositions — "göre" — according to
explanation:
This chapter focuses only on "göre." The other postpositions are covered in their own separate chapters, so the exercises here won't mix them in.

göre means "according to." Unlike "için," it always takes the DATIVE case on the noun or pronoun in front of it — no genitive exception for pronouns:

  • bu habere göre = according to this news (haber + dative -e)
  • bana göre = according to me (dative bana, from ben)
  • Sana göre en iyi film hangisi? = In your opinion (according to you), which is the best film?

"göre" is also used for comparison relative to a changing standard, similar to English "compared to":

  • Geçen yıla göre daha sıcak. = It's warmer compared to last year.

In the exercises, you'll practise "göre" with the dative case, on both nouns and pronouns.

title: Postpositions — "rağmen" — despite
explanation:
This chapter focuses only on "rağmen." The other postpositions are covered in their own separate chapters, so the exercises here won't mix them in.

rağmen means "despite/although." Like "göre," it always takes the DATIVE case — no genitive exception for pronouns:

  • yağmura rağmen = despite the rain (yağmur + dative -a)
  • buna rağmen = despite this (dative buna, from bu)
  • Yorgunluğuna rağmen çalışmaya devam etti. = Despite his tiredness, he kept working.

To say "despite doing/being something" with a full clause, attach rağmen to -mesine/-masına (a verbal noun + dative):

  • Hastalanmasına rağmen okula gitti. = Despite getting sick, he went to school.

In the exercises, you'll practise "rağmen" with the dative case, on nouns, pronouns, and full clauses.

title: Adverbs — Formation & Position
explanation:
An adverb describes how, when, or where an action happens — it modifies a verb rather than a noun. In English, we usually mark this with -ly (quick → quickly). Turkish is looser: very often the adjective form is simply reused as-is, with no ending change at all.

This means many Turkish words do double duty as both adjective and adverb, and only the position in the sentence (right before the verb) tells you which job they're doing.

  • iyi = good (adjective) / well (adverb) — iyi bir kitap (a good book) vs. iyi konuşuyor (he speaks well)
  • hızlı = fast (adjective) / fast, quickly (adverb) — hızlı araba (fast car) vs. hızlı koşuyor (he runs fast)
  • güzel = beautiful / nicely — güzel resim (beautiful picture) vs. güzel yazıyor (she writes nicely)
  • yavaş = slow / slowly — yavaş yavaş (slowly, little by little)

Some adjectives can also take the suffix -ca/-ce (following two-way vowel harmony) to explicitly form an adverb, giving a slightly more formal or emphatic "in a ... manner" feel:

  • -ca (after back vowels: a, ı, o, u)
  • -ce (after front vowels: e, i, ö, ü)
  • hızlı + ca → hızlıca = quickly, rather quickly
  • kolay + ca → kolayca = easily
  • güzel + ce → güzelce = nicely, properly
  • sessiz + ce → sessizce = silently

Both forms often exist side by side, and the plain adjective-as-adverb version is usually the more everyday, spoken choice:

  • Hızlı koştu. = He ran fast.
  • Hızlıca koştu. = He ran quickly. (slightly more descriptive/literary)

Word order matters more than shape here: an adverb normally sits directly before the verb it modifies, near the end of the sentence, since Turkish verbs come last.

  • Yavaş yürüyor. = He is walking slowly.
  • Çok iyi anlıyorum. = I understand very well.
  • Sessizce kapıyı açtı. = She opened the door silently.
  • Bugün erken geldi. = He came early today.

Turkish also has a set of adverbs that never had an adjective form to begin with — these are just learned as vocabulary: çok (very/a lot), az (little), her zaman (always), bazen (sometimes), hemen (immediately). These behave exactly like the ones above: they sit before the word they describe.

Unlike the demonstrative pronouns bu/şu/o from the previous lesson, which change form for case and number because they act as nouns, adverbs never take case or plural endings — they're invariable, no matter where they appear in the sentence.

A useful mnemonic is the question an adverb answers:

Nasıl? = How?

  • Nasıl konuşuyor? — How does he speak?
  • Güzel konuşuyor. — He speaks nicely.

In the exercises, you'll practise telling adjective and adverb uses apart, forming -ca/-ce adverbs correctly, and placing adverbs naturally before the verb.

title: Future Tense -ecek
explanation:
The future tense suffix -ecek/-acak describes actions that will happen — things planned, predicted, or expected to take place after now. It's the direct match for English "will" or "am/is/are going to."

Like other tense suffixes, it attaches straight onto the verb stem, and then personal endings attach after it to show who's doing the action.

The suffix has two forms, following two-way vowel harmony:

  • -ecek (after front vowels: e, i, ö, ü)
  • -acak (after back vowels: a, ı, o, u)

Basic examples (with personal endings attached):

  • gel + ecek + im → geleceğim = I will come
  • bak + acak + sın → bakacaksın = you will look
  • gid + ecek → gidecek = he/she will go
  • oku + yacak + ız → okuyacağız = we will read

Two extra rules make future forms slightly trickier than a plain suffix attachment:

1. The final "k" softens to "ğ" before a vowel-starting personal ending (the 1st person singular/plural endings -im and -iz start with a vowel):

  • gelecek + im → geleceğim = I will come (k → ğ)
  • gelecek + iz → geleceğiz = we will come (k → ğ)
  • bakacak + ım → bakacağım = I will look (k → ğ)

Notice this softening does not happen before -sın, -sınız, or in the plain 3rd person form — only before endings that start with a vowel.

2. A buffer "-y-" appears if the verb stem ends in a vowel (Turkish never allows two vowels to collide):

  • oku + yacak → okuyacak = he/she will read
  • bekle + yecek → bekleyecek = he/she will wait
  • anla + yacağım → anlayacağım = I will understand

Examples in full sentences:

  • Yarın geleceğim. = I will come tomorrow.
  • Okula gidecek. = He/she will go to school.
  • Onu bekleyeceğiz. = We will wait for him/her.
  • Ne yapacaksın? = What will you do?

A useful mnemonic is the question the future tense answers:

Ne zaman? = When? / Ne yapacaksın? = What will you do?

  • Ne zaman geleceksin? — When will you come?
  • Yarın geleceğim. — I will come tomorrow.

Compare with the ablative case you just learned: that suffix marks "from" a place, while this one marks a moment in time yet to happen — different kind of marker, but the same habit of glueing meaning directly onto a word rather than using a separate helper word like English "will."

In the exercises, you'll practise building correct future forms across persons, including the k→ğ softening and the buffer -y- where the stem ends in a vowel.

title: Comparison (daha, en, kadar, gibi) — "daha" — comparative
explanation:
This chapter focuses only on the "daha" — comparative form. The other comparison words are covered in their own separate chapters, so the exercises here won't mix them in.

daha means "more"/"-er" — it makes a comparative. The thing being compared to takes the ABLATIVE case (-den/-dan), and word order is: [standard + ablative] / daha / adjective:

  • Bu ev ondan daha büyük. = This house is bigger than that (one).
  • Ben senden daha genç değilim. = I'm not younger than you.
  • Daha alone (no ablative standard mentioned) just means "more": Daha su ister misin? = Do you want more water?

In the exercises, you'll practise building comparative sentences with an ablative standard of comparison and "daha."

title: Comparison (daha, en, kadar, gibi) — "en" — superlative
explanation:
This chapter focuses only on the "en" — superlative form. The other comparison words are covered in their own separate chapters, so the exercises here won't mix them in.

en means "the most" — it makes a superlative. Unlike "daha," it takes no case suffix on anything; it just sits directly before the adjective:

  • en büyük = the biggest
  • Bu, sınıftaki en zeki öğrenci. = This is the smartest student in the class.
  • Türkiye'nin en kalabalık şehri İstanbul'dur. = Turkey's most crowded city is Istanbul.

In the exercises, you'll practise building superlative phrases and sentences with "en."

title: Comparison (daha, en, kadar, gibi) — "kadar" — as...as
explanation:
This chapter focuses only on the "kadar" — equative (as...as) form. The other comparison words, and the separate temporal use of "kadar" ("until"), are covered in their own chapters, so the exercises here won't mix them in.

kadar here means "as...as" — an equative comparison of equal degree. The standard of comparison takes NO case suffix (unlike "daha," which needs the ablative), and word order is: standard / kadar / adjective:

  • Senin kadar uzunum. = I'm as tall as you.
  • Bu kitap o kitap kadar ilginç değil. = This book isn't as interesting as that book.
  • Onun kadar hızlı koşamam. = I can't run as fast as him.

In the exercises, you'll practise equative comparisons with "kadar."

title: Comparison (daha, en, kadar, gibi) — "kadar" — until/as far as
explanation:
This chapter focuses only on the "kadar" — temporal (until) form. The equative comparison use of "kadar" ("as...as"), and the other comparison words, are covered in their own separate chapters, so the exercises here won't mix them in.

The same word kadar also means "until" when it follows a time expression or a place — a completely different function from the equative "as...as" you may already know:

  • Akşama kadar burada olacağım. = I'll be here until evening.
  • Saat beşe kadar çalışıyorum. = I work until five o'clock.

With a VERB instead of a time noun, attach kadar to the verb's -(y)IncAyA + dative-marked infinitive-like form, meaning "until [something happens]":

  • Eve varana kadar bekle. = Wait until (I/you) get home.
  • O gelene kadar burada kal. = Stay here until he comes.

In the exercises, you'll practise "kadar" meaning "until," with both time nouns and verb-based clauses.

title: Comparison (daha, en, kadar, gibi) — "gibi" — like/as
explanation:
This chapter focuses only on the "gibi" — simile form. The other comparison words are covered in their own separate chapters, so the exercises here won't mix them in.

gibi means "like"/"as" — a simile/resemblance. The noun it follows takes NO case suffix, EXCEPT a personal pronoun, which takes the GENITIVE (the same quirk you may have met with "için"):

  • aslan gibi = like a lion (bare noun)
  • Çocuk gibi davranıyorsun. = You're behaving like a child.
  • benim gibi = like me (genitive benim, NOT the bare "ben gibi")
  • Senin gibi düşünmüyorum. = I don't think like you (do).

In the exercises, you'll practise similes with "gibi," on both plain nouns and personal pronouns.

title: Conjunctions — "ki" — complementizer "that"
explanation:
This chapter focuses only on "ki" as a relative "that"-clause linker. The other senses of "ki," and the other conjunctions, are covered in their own separate chapters, so the exercises here won't mix them in.

Borrowed from Persian, ki can link two clauses the way English "that" does — unusually for Turkish, this "ki" clause comes AFTER the verb it explains, not before (Turkish is normally verb-final, so this is a genuine exception):

  • Bilirim ki sen haklısın. = I know that you're right.
  • Duydum ki yeni bir iş bulmuş. = I heard that he found a new job.
  • Umarım ki her şey yolundadır. = I hope that everything is fine.

This "ki" is more common in slightly formal or written Turkish; everyday speech often prefers the native construction with -diğini (a verbal noun + possessive), which you'll meet in indirect speech.

In the exercises, you'll practise linking a main clause to a "that"-clause with "ki."

title: Conjunctions — "ki" — purpose "so that"
explanation:
This chapter focuses only on "ki" expressing purpose ("so that"). The other senses of "ki," and the other conjunctions, are covered in their own separate chapters, so the exercises here won't mix them in.

ki can also introduce a purpose clause, "so that...," typically followed by a verb in the optative (-e/-eyim) mood:

  • Erken geldim ki seni görebileyim. = I came early so that I could see you.
  • Sessiz ol ki bebek uyusun. = Be quiet so that the baby (can) sleep.

This is less common than the native -mek için purpose construction you already know ("Seni görmek için erken geldim" means almost the same thing), but "ki" for purpose does still appear, especially in more deliberate or slightly formal speech.

In the exercises, you'll practise purpose clauses with "ki."

title: Conjunctions — "ki" — result "so...that"
explanation:
This chapter focuses only on "ki" expressing result ("so...that"). The other senses of "ki," and the other conjunctions, are covered in their own separate chapters, so the exercises here won't mix them in.

ki also links a degree word (o kadar/öyle, "so") to its result: "so [adjective] that [result]." The intensity word comes first, "ki" links to the consequence:

  • O kadar yoruldum ki uyuyakaldım. = I got so tired that I fell asleep.
  • Öyle güzel bir gündü ki dışarı çıktık. = It was such a beautiful day that we went outside.
  • O kadar hızlı konuştu ki anlayamadım. = He spoke so fast that I couldn't understand.

In the exercises, you'll practise "o kadar/öyle ... ki ..." result clauses.

title: Conjunctions — "ki" — surprise/realization
explanation:
This chapter focuses only on "ki" for rhetorical surprise/emphasis. The other senses of "ki," and the other conjunctions, are covered in their own separate chapters, so the exercises here won't mix them in.

"ki" can also sit at the end of a clause to add emphasis, indignation, or rhetorical surprise — often in a question that isn't really asking for information, but pushing back or expressing disbelief:

  • Sen kimsin ki bana böyle konuşuyorsun? = Who are you (anyway) to talk to me like this?
  • Param yok ki alayım! = I don't have any money to buy it (with)! (frustration/emphasis)
  • Ne bileyim ki? = How should I know?! (rhetorical)

This use is hard to translate word-for-word — it's a tone/attitude marker more than a literal meaning, so pay attention to the emotional flavor (indignation, disbelief, exasperation) rather than trying to render "ki" itself in English.

In the exercises, you'll practise this emphatic/rhetorical use of "ki."

title: Conjunctions — hem...hem — both...and
explanation:
This chapter focuses only on "hem...hem (de)." The other conjunctions are covered in their own separate chapters, so the exercises here won't mix them in.

hem...hem (de) means "both...and" — it links two parallel qualities, actions, or items, each preceded by its own "hem":

  • Hem yorgunum hem açım. = I'm both tired and hungry.
  • Hem çalışıyor hem de okuyor. = He's both working and studying (the "de" on the second hem is optional, adds a touch of emphasis).
  • Hem sen hem ben gideceğiz. = Both you and I will go.

In the exercises, you'll practise linking two parallel items or clauses with "hem...hem (de)."

title: Conjunctions — ya...ya — either...or
explanation:
This chapter focuses only on "ya...ya (da)." The other conjunctions are covered in their own separate chapters, so the exercises here won't mix them in.

ya...ya (da) means "either...or" — it presents two alternatives, each preceded by its own "ya":

  • Ya gel ya git. = Either come or go (don't just stand there).
  • Ya çay ya da kahve içerim. = I'll drink either tea or coffee.
  • Ya bugün ya yarın bitiririm. = I'll finish either today or tomorrow.

The "da/de" on the second "ya" is optional, much like with "hem...hem de" — it's slightly more common in writing than dropping it, but both are fine.

In the exercises, you'll practise presenting two alternatives with "ya...ya (da)."

title: Instrumental Case (-(y)la/-(y)le) — instrumental — with a tool
explanation:
This chapter focuses only on the instrumental sense (with a tool/means). The other senses are covered in their own separate chapters, so the exercises here won't mix them in.

The instrumental case suffix -(y)la/-(y)le (2-way harmony, buffer -y- after a vowel) is the attached form of the postposition ile. Here it answers "with what/by what means":

  • kalemle yazdım = I wrote with a pen
  • otobüsle geldim = I came by bus
  • bıçakla kesti = he cut it with a knife

In the exercises, you'll practise -(y)la/-(y)le meaning "with"/"by means of" a tool or method.

title: Instrumental Case (-(y)la/-(y)le) — comitative — with a person
explanation:
This chapter focuses only on the comitative sense (with a person). The other senses are covered in their own separate chapters, so the exercises here won't mix them in.

The same suffix -(y)la/-(y)le also answers "with whom" — accompaniment, rather than a tool:

  • arkadaşımla geldim = I came with my friend
  • seninle konuşmak istiyorum = I want to talk with you
  • annemle alışverişe gittim = I went shopping with my mother

In the exercises, you'll practise -(y)la/-(y)le meaning "with" a person (accompaniment).

title: Instrumental Case (-(y)la/-(y)le) — conjunction — and
explanation:
This chapter focuses only on the conjunctive sense ("and"). The other senses are covered in their own separate chapters, so the exercises here won't mix them in.

The same suffix -(y)la/-(y)le can also link two nouns the way ve ("and") does, joining them into one tight pair:

  • çayla kahve = tea and coffee
  • anne ve babamla is NOT how this works — you attach -(y)la only to the FIRST noun of the pair: annem ve babam = my mother and father, but annemle babam = my mother and (my) father, same meaning, more casual/spoken style

In the exercises, you'll practise -(y)la/-(y)le linking two nouns like "and."

title: Emphasis Particles — "de/da" — also/too
explanation:
This chapter focuses only on additive "de/da" (also/too). The other senses of "de/da," and the other emphasis particles, are covered in their own separate chapters, so the exercises here won't mix them in.

Written as a SEPARATE word (2-way harmony, never attached), de/da most commonly means "also/too" — adding the marked word to a set:

  • Ben de geliyorum. = I'm coming too.
  • O da öğrenci. = He's a student too.
  • Bunu da al. = Take this one too.

Note "de/da" attaches its meaning to whichever word it directly follows — moving it changes what's being added: "Ben de geliyorum" (I'm ALSO coming) vs "Ben geliyorum da" would emphasize something else entirely.

In the exercises, you'll practise "de/da" meaning "also/too."

title: Emphasis Particles — "de/da" — contrastive
explanation:
This chapter focuses only on contrastive "de/da" (but/and yet). The other senses of "de/da," and the other emphasis particles, are covered in their own separate chapters, so the exercises here won't mix them in.

The same word de/da can also work like a light "but/and yet," softening a contrast between two clauses — milder than ama:

  • Çalıştı da geçemedi. = He studied, but still couldn't pass.
  • Aradım da açmadı. = I called, but he didn't pick up.

In the exercises, you'll practise "de/da" linking two clauses in a mild contrast.

title: Emphasis Particles — "de/da" — rhetorical emphasis
explanation:
This chapter focuses only on intensifying "de/da" in exclamations. The other senses of "de/da," and the other emphasis particles, are covered in their own separate chapters, so the exercises here won't mix them in.

After a question word like ne ("what/how"), de/da intensifies an exclamation — "how very...!":

  • Ne de güzel bir gün! = What a beautiful day!
  • Ne de çok yağmur yağıyor! = It's raining SO much!

In the exercises, you'll practise "ne de" exclamations.

title: Emphasis Particles — "bile" — even
explanation:
This chapter focuses only on "bile" (even). The other emphasis particles are covered in their own separate chapters, so the exercises here won't mix them in.

bile means "even" — it marks the most extreme/unexpected item in a set, usually after the word it emphasizes:

  • Bunu bile bilmiyor. = He doesn't even know this.
  • Çocuklar bile anladı. = Even the children understood.
  • Bakmadı bile. = He didn't even look.

In the exercises, you'll practise "bile" for "even."

title: Emphasis Particles — "üstelik" — moreover
explanation:
This chapter focuses only on "üstelik" (moreover). The other emphasis particles are covered in their own separate chapters, so the exercises here won't mix them in.

üstelik means "moreover/on top of that" — it introduces an additional, often aggravating, fact at the START of a clause:

  • Üstelik geç de kaldı. = Moreover, he was also late.
  • Param yok, üstelik hastayım. = I have no money, and on top of that, I'm sick.

In the exercises, you'll practise "üstelik" introducing an additional point.

title: Emphasis Particles — "hatta" — in fact/even
explanation:
This chapter focuses only on "hatta" (in fact/even). The other emphasis particles are covered in their own separate chapters, so the exercises here won't mix them in.

hatta means "in fact/even" — it introduces a stronger, more surprising follow-up to what was just said, at the START of a clause:

  • Hatta bana yardım etti. = He even helped me (in fact).
  • Çok yorgunum, hatta uyuyakalabilirim. = I'm very tired — I might even fall asleep.

Unlike "bile" (which attaches right after the emphasized word), "hatta" sits at the start of its own clause, adding a whole new, stronger point.

In the exercises, you'll practise "hatta" introducing a stronger follow-up.

title: Indefinite Pronouns & Quantifiers
explanation:
Indefinite pronouns and quantifiers let you talk about people or things without naming them exactly — "someone," "everyone," "no one," "some," "every." Turkish has a small, sturdy set of these words, and once you learn them, they behave very predictably.

Unlike the suffixes you've been learning (locative, dative, instrumental...), most of these are separate words that you place before a noun or use on their own as a pronoun. A few of them do take case suffixes when used as pronouns, though — so this lesson connects with everything you've already learned.

The core set to know:

  • biri / birisi = someone
  • bir şey = something
  • herkes = everyone
  • her şey = everything
  • hiç kimse / kimse = no one
  • hiçbir şey = nothing
  • bazı = some (used before a noun)
  • her = every (used before a noun, singular)

Basic examples:

  • Biri geldi. = Someone came.
  • Herkes biliyor. = Everyone knows.
  • Bazı öğrenciler geldi. = Some students came.
  • Her gün koşuyorum. = I run every day.

A few points that trip learners up:

1. "Her" always pairs with a singular noun, even though the meaning feels plural in English:

  • her gün = every day (not "her günler")
  • her çocuk = every child
  • her ev = every house

2. "Kimse" and "hiçbir şey" need a negative verb to mean "no one / nothing" — Turkish, like Spanish, uses double negation here:

  • Kimse gelmedi. = No one came. (literally "no-one didn't-come")
  • Hiçbir şey görmedim. = I saw nothing.
  • Kimse yok. = There's no one (here). (yok is itself already "there isn't")

3. As pronouns, these words take case suffixes just like any noun, following the same vowel harmony and buffer rules you already know:

  • birine = to someone (biri + dative -e, with buffer -n-)
  • herkese = to everyone (herkes + dative -e)
  • kimseyle = with no one (kimse + instrumental -yle)
  • birisiyle konuştum = I talked with someone (birisi + instrumental -yle)

That last example connects directly to the instrumental case from the previous lesson: exactly the same -(y)la/-(y)le suffix you just learned attaches to these pronouns without any special exception.

Full sentence examples:

  • Bazı insanlar anlamıyor. = Some people don't understand.
  • Her şeyi biliyorsun. = You know everything.
  • Kimseyi görmedim. = I didn't see anyone.
  • Birisi seni arıyor. = Someone is looking for you.
  • Herkes mutlu. = Everyone is happy.

A useful mnemonic is the question these words often answer:

Kim? = Who? / Ne? = What?

  • Kim geldi? — Who came? Kimse gelmedi. — No one came.
  • Ne oldu? — What happened? Hiçbir şey olmadı. — Nothing happened.

In the exercises, you'll practise choosing the right indefinite pronoun or quantifier, matching negative verbs with kimse/hiçbir şey, and attaching case suffixes to these words correctly.

title: Past Tense -miş (Hearsay/Inferred) — hearsay
explanation:
This chapter focuses only on the hearsay sense of -miş. The other senses are covered in their own separate chapters, so the exercises here won't mix them in.

-miş (4-way harmony) marks that you are reporting something you were TOLD, not something you witnessed yourself:

  • Ali gelmiş. = I heard/was told Ali came (I didn't see it myself).
  • Yeni bir iş bulmuşsun, tebrikler! = I heard you found a new job, congrats! (secondhand info)

Compare with the plain, witnessed -di past: Ali geldi (Ali came — I saw it) vs. Ali gelmiş (Ali apparently came — I only heard about it).

In the exercises, you'll practise -miş reporting secondhand information.

title: Past Tense -miş (Hearsay/Inferred) — inferential
explanation:
This chapter focuses only on the inferential sense of -miş. The other senses are covered in their own separate chapters, so the exercises here won't mix them in.

The same -miş also marks a conclusion drawn from visible evidence, rather than something you were told or witnessed directly:

  • Yağmur yağmış. = It must have rained (I see the wet ground, but didn't see it rain).
  • Birisi burada yemek yapmış. = Someone has clearly cooked here (judging by the smell/mess).

In the exercises, you'll practise -miş drawing a conclusion from evidence.

title: Past Tense -miş (Hearsay/Inferred) — surprise/mirative
explanation:
This chapter focuses only on the mirative (surprise) sense of -miş. The other senses are covered in their own separate chapters, so the exercises here won't mix them in.

-miş can also mark your own surprise at something you've just discovered about the present or the past — a realization, not really a report about someone else:

  • Param bitmiş! = Oh, my money's run out! (I just noticed)
  • Sen ne kadar büyümüşsün! = Wow, how much you've grown! (surprised realization on seeing someone)

In the exercises, you'll practise -miş expressing surprise at a sudden realization.

title: Necessitative -meli (Must/Should) — Present (-meli)
explanation:
This chapter focuses only on the present (-meli) form. The other forms are covered in their own separate chapters, so the exercises here won't mix them in.

-meli/-malı (2-way harmony) means "must/should," attached directly to the verb stem:

  • Gitmeliyim. = I must go.
  • Erken kalkmalısın. = You should get up early.
  • Bunu görmeli. = He/she must see this.

The negative inserts -me- before -meli: Gitmemeliyim = I must not go.

In the exercises, you'll practise the present necessitative, positive and negative.

title: Necessitative -meli (Must/Should) — Past (-meliydi)
explanation:
This chapter focuses only on the past (-meliydi) form. The other forms are covered in their own separate chapters, so the exercises here won't mix them in.

Adding the past copula -ydi to -meli gives -meliydi: "should have.../had to..." — a retrospective judgment about something that did or didn't happen:

  • Gitmeliydim. = I should have gone (implying I didn't, or judging that I had to).
  • Erken kalkmalıydın. = You should have gotten up early.
  • Bunu bilmeliydi. = He/she should have known this.

In the exercises, you'll practise the past necessitative, expressing hindsight obligation.

title: Necessitative -meli (Must/Should) — Questions (mi/mı/mu/mü)
explanation:
This chapter focuses only on yes/no questions with -meli. Statement forms are covered in their own separate chapters, so the exercises here focus on the question pattern itself.

Add the question particle mi/mı/mu/mü as a separate word after -meli, with the personal ending on the particle:

  • Gitmeli miyim? = Must I go?
  • Şimdi karar vermeli miyiz? = Must we decide now?
  • Bunu yapmalı mıydın? = Did you really have to do this? (past necessitative question)

In the exercises, you'll practise turning necessitative statements into yes/no questions.

title: Past Continuous
explanation:
The past continuous describes an action that was in progress at some point in the past — the Turkish equivalent of English "was/were -ing". It's built by taking the present-continuous marker -iyor you already know and adding past-tense endings onto it, instead of the personal endings you've used so far.

Structure: verb stem + -iyor + past marker (-du/-dı/-dü/-tu, etc.) + personal ending.

Personal endings on gelmek (to come):

  • geliyordum = I was coming
  • geliyordun = you were coming
  • geliyordu = he/she/it was coming
  • geliyorduk = we were coming
  • geliyordunuz = you (plural/formal) were coming
  • geliyorlardı = they were coming

Notice the past marker itself doesn't shift with four-way vowel harmony here, because it's always attached after the fixed -iyor — it just alternates between -du and -dü (and -tu/-tü after certain endings), matching only the front/back quality of the last vowel in -iyor, which is always the back-ish "o" sound, so in practice you'll almost always see -du/-tu here.

More examples:

  • okuyordu = he/she was reading
  • yazıyordum = I was writing
  • çalışıyorduk = we were working
  • bekliyordunuz = you were waiting

Just like in English, this tense is used to set the scene for something else that happened, often interrupting the ongoing action:

  • Ben kitap okuyordum. = I was reading a book.
  • O gelirken ben yemek yapıyordum. = I was cooking when he was arriving.
  • Dün akşam televizyon izliyordum. = I was watching TV last night.
  • Telefon çaldığında uyuyorduk. = We were sleeping when the phone rang.

This makes the past continuous the backbone of storytelling in Turkish — it paints the background action, while a simple past-tense verb usually supplies the event that interrupts it.

A quick contrast worth keeping in mind: geldim (I came — a completed action) vs. geliyordum (I was coming — an action in progress). The suffix stack tells you exactly which one you mean, the same way emphasis particles like de/da or mi from the previous lesson attach onto a word to add precise shades of meaning rather than needing separate words.

In the exercises, you'll practice conjugating verbs in the past continuous across different persons and recognizing it in short narrative sentences.

title: Conditional -se (If) — Verb conditional (-se/-sa)
explanation:
This chapter focuses only on the verb conditional (-se/-sa). The noun/adjective conditional is covered in its own separate chapter, so the exercises here won't mix it in.

-se/-sa (2-way harmony) attaches directly to a VERB stem to mean "if":

  • Gelirse söyle. = If he comes, tell (me).
  • Yağmur yağarsa gitmeyiz. = If it rains, we won't go.
  • Param olsa, yeni bir araba alırdım. = If I had money, I'd buy a new car (a further hypothetical layer, "olsa" itself is just "if [there] were").

In the exercises, you'll practise -se/-sa attached directly to verbs.

title: Conditional -se (If) — Noun/adjective conditional (olursa/ise)
explanation:
This chapter focuses only on the noun/adjective conditional (ise/-se copula). The verb conditional is covered in its own separate chapter, so the exercises here won't mix it in.

To say "if" about a NOUN or ADJECTIVE predicate (not a verb), use the conditional copula ise, usually attached as -(y)se/-(y)sa:

  • Hasta ise, gelmesin. / Hastaysa, gelmesin. = If he's sick, he shouldn't come.
  • Öğrenciyse indirim var. = If (he's) a student, there's a discount.
  • Bu doğruysa çok kötü. = If this is true, (that's) very bad.

In the exercises, you'll practise the conditional copula on noun/adjective predicates.

title: The Optative (Wish)
explanation:
The optative mood expresses a wish, suggestion, or self-directed intention — "let me...", "let's...", "may...". English doesn't have a single dedicated form for this; it borrows the verb let ("let me go", "let's go") or the modal may ("may he live long"). Turkish instead builds it right into the verb with a suffix.

The optative is mostly used in the first person (I / we), where it means "let me..." or "let's...". It attaches directly to the verb stem, after any negation, and follows two-way vowel harmony:

  • -eyim / -ayım (I) — after front vowels: -eyim; after back vowels: -ayım
  • -elim / -alım (we) — after front vowels: -elim; after back vowels: -alım

Basic examples:

  • gideyim = let me go
  • gidelim = let's go
  • bakayım = let me look / let me see
  • yapalım = let's do (it)
  • yiyeyim = let me eat

The third person also has optative forms, though they're rarer and closer in feel to English "may" or "let him/her/them":

  • gitsin = let him/her go
  • gitsinler = let them go

Negation works by inserting -me/-ma before the optative suffix, just as it does with other verb forms:

  • gitmeyeyim = let me not go / I'd better not go
  • bakmayalım = let's not look

Examples in full sentences:

  • Ben de geleyim mi? = Should I come too? / Shall I come too?
  • Hadi, gidelim! = Come on, let's go!
  • Bir daha deneyeyim. = Let me try one more time.
  • Yarın buluşalım. = Let's meet up tomorrow.
  • Ona sormayayım. = Let me not ask him/her. / Maybe I shouldn't ask him/her.

Notice how naturally the optative pairs with the question particle mi/mı/mu/mü: asking "Geleyim mi?" ("Should I come?") is a very common way to offer to do something or check if a suggestion is welcome, much more common than phrasing it as a plain statement.

Compare this with the past continuous you just learned: that tense described an ongoing action actually happening in the past (gidiyordum = I was going), while the optative doesn't describe reality at all — it proposes or wishes for an action, tied to no particular time.

In the exercises, you'll practise forming first-person optative suggestions and wishes, including their negative forms, and using them naturally with "mi" to offer or propose something.

title: The Suffix -ki
explanation:
The suffix -ki turns a noun (usually already in the genitive or locative case) into something that behaves like an adjective or pronoun — it lets you say "the one belonging to..." or "the one that is [somewhere]" without repeating the noun you're referring back to.

Don't confuse it with the conjunction ki ("that") from the earlier conjunctions lesson — that one is a separate connecting word, while this -ki is a suffix glued onto a noun form.

Unlike most Turkish suffixes, -ki mostly ignores vowel harmony — it usually stays -ki regardless of the vowels in the word, though after a rounded-vowel word it can appear as -kü or -kı in a few fixed forms (like bugünkü = "today's"). For most learning purposes, just treat it as -ki.

1. Possessive use — attached to genitive pronouns/nouns: it replaces a noun you'd otherwise have to repeat, similar to English "mine" instead of "my book".

  • benim + ki → benimki = my one → mine
  • senin + ki → seninki = your one → yours
  • Ali'nin + ki → Ali'ninki = Ali's one → Ali's

2. Relative/locational use — attached to a locative form: it turns "at/in/on X" into "the one at/in/on X", letting it describe a following noun like an adjective.

  • masada + ki → masadaki = on the table + -ki → the one on the table
  • evde + ki → evdeki = at home + -ki → the one at home
  • okulda + ki → okuldaki = at school + -ki → the one at school

Full-sentence examples:

  • Bu araba benimki. = This car is mine.
  • Seninki nerede? = Where is yours?
  • Masadaki kitap benim. = The book on the table is mine.
  • Evdeki çocuklar uyuyor. = The children at home are sleeping.
  • Cebimdeki para az. = The money in my pocket is little (I don't have much money in my pocket).

Notice the pattern: in the relative use, -ki almost always follows a locative form (-de/-da), and the resulting word sits before a noun just like an adjective — masadaki kitap literally builds "table-at-ki book" into "the book that is on the table".

In the exercises, you'll practise building -ki forms from possessive and locative words, and using them both as standalone pronouns ("mine") and as modifiers before a noun ("the one on the table").

title: The Reflexive Pronoun Kendi — reflexive object
explanation:
This chapter focuses only on kendi as a reflexive object. The other uses are covered in their own separate chapters, so the exercises here won't mix them in.

kendi ("self") takes a possessive suffix + case suffix to work as a reflexive OBJECT — "myself/yourself/himself...":

  • Kendimi gördüm. = I saw myself. (kendi + m + i, accusative)
  • Kendine iyi bak. = Take good care of yourself. (kendi + n + e, dative)
  • Kendinden bahsetsene. = Why don't you tell (me) about yourself. (kendi + n + den, ablative)

This is distinct from the reflexive verb suffix -in you may meet elsewhere (e.g. "yıkandım" = I washed myself, built into the verb) — "kendi" is a separate pronoun-like word, usable with any case.

In the exercises, you'll practise "kendi" + possessive + case suffix as a reflexive object.

title: The Reflexive Pronoun Kendi — emphatic
explanation:
This chapter focuses only on the emphatic use of kendi. The other uses are covered in their own separate chapters, so the exercises here won't mix them in.

kendi + possessive can also stand ALONGSIDE a subject pronoun to add emphasis — "...myself/personally," underlining that the subject did it without help or in person:

  • Ben kendim yaptım. = I did it myself.
  • Sen kendin söyle. = Say it yourself.
  • Kendisi geldi. = He came himself/in person.

In the exercises, you'll practise "kendi" + possessive used for emphasis alongside a subject.

title: The Reflexive Pronoun Kendi — possessive "own"
explanation:
This chapter focuses only on kendi meaning "own." The other uses are covered in their own separate chapters, so the exercises here won't mix them in.

kendi + possessive placed before a noun means "my/your/... OWN [noun]" — emphasizing ownership/independence rather than reflexivity:

  • Kendi evim var. = I have my own house.
  • Kendi arabanla mı geldin? = Did you come in your own car?
  • Herkes kendi işine baksın. = Everyone should mind their own business.

In the exercises, you'll practise "kendi" + possessive meaning "own" before a noun.

title: Converb: Without/Before Doing
explanation:
Turkish has a special verb form called a converb — a non-finite verb that links two actions together without needing a separate word for "and" or "before." This lesson covers the converb that means "without doing X", and how to extend it to mean "before doing X."

This replaces English constructions like "without eating" or "before going" — instead of a preposition + -ing form, Turkish just glues a suffix onto the verb stem.

The suffix is -madan/-meden, attached directly to the bare verb stem, following two-way vowel harmony:

  • -madan (after back vowels: a, ı, o, u)
  • -meden (after front vowels: e, i, ö, ü)

Basic examples:

  • yemeden = without eating
  • gitmeden = without going
  • görmeden = without seeing
  • okumadan = without reading
  • konuşmadan = without speaking

1. Add "önce" to mean "before doing X." The converb form doesn't change — you simply place önce ("before") right after it:

  • gitmeden önce = before going
  • yemeden önce = before eating
  • uyumadan önce = before sleeping

2. Watch out for the negative suffix look-alike. This is the exact same shape as the negative marker -me/-ma (as in gitmedi — "he didn't go"). Context tells them apart: the negative marker attaches to a fully conjugated verb with its own tense/person endings, while the converb -madan/-meden stands alone on the stem and always links to another clause.

Examples in full sentences:

  • Yemeden gitti. = He left without eating.
  • Kitabı okumadan filmi izledim. = I watched the movie without reading the book.
  • Eve gitmeden önce markete uğradım. = Before going home, I stopped by the market.
  • Düşünmeden konuştu. = He spoke without thinking.
  • Uyumadan önce kitap okurum. = Before sleeping, I read a book.

Compare this with the suffix -ki from the previous lesson: both attach directly and change a word's grammatical role, but where -ki turns a place/time expression into an adjective, -madan/-meden turns a verb into a linking form that connects two actions in one sentence.

In the exercises, you'll practise forming -madan/-meden from verb stems, telling it apart from the negative suffix, and adding önce to express "before doing" something.

title: Converb -DIktan Sonra (After Doing)
explanation:
The suffix -DIktan sonra means "after doing [something]". It attaches directly to a verb stem to turn it into a time expression, letting you link two actions without starting a new sentence — much like English "after eating, I..." or "after he came home, ...".

Unlike a normal tense ending, this form doesn't change with person — it stays the same no matter who's doing the action, because the person is usually clear from the rest of the sentence (or can be added separately, as you'll see below).

The suffix has two parts: -DIk (a four-way vowel-harmony suffix, also voicing to -tık/-tik/-tuk/-tük after unvoiced consonants) plus the fixed word sonra (after):

  • -dıktan sonra (after: a, ı)
  • -dikten sonra (after: e, i)
  • -duktan sonra (after: o, u)
  • -dükten sonra (after: ö, ü)
  • -tıktan/-tikten/-tuktan/-tükten sonra (after unvoiced consonants: p, ç, t, k, s, ş, h, f)

Basic examples:

  • yemek yedikten sonra = after eating (food)
  • eve geldikten sonra = after coming home
  • okuduktan sonra = after reading
  • çalıştıktan sonra = after working
  • uyuduktan sonra = after sleeping

Notice the pattern: take the verb stem, add -DIk with the right vowel (and consonant, if the stem ends unvoiced), then simply attach sonra. No tense marker or personal ending is needed inside the word itself.

Full sentence examples:

  • Yemek yedikten sonra dışarı çıktım. = After eating, I went outside.
  • Eve geldikten sonra duş aldı. = After coming home, he/she took a shower.
  • Kitabı okuduktan sonra sana vereceğim. = After I read the book, I'll give it to you.
  • Çalıştıktan sonra çok yorulduk. = After working, we got very tired.

If you need to be explicit about who does the first action (especially when it's a different person from the main clause), add a possessive-style ending before sonra: ben geldikten sonra = after I came, o gittikten sonra = after he/she left. But in most everyday sentences, the plain form above is enough.

This suffix is the mirror image of -madan önce ("before doing"), which you may already know: yemekten önce (before eating) vs. yedikten sonra (after eating). Where -madan önce uses the negative-looking stem plus "before", -DIktan sonra uses the "-DIk" stem plus "after" — same slot in the sentence, opposite meaning in time.

A useful mnemonic is the question it answers: Ne zaman? = When? / Neden sonra? = After what?

  • Ne zaman dışarı çıktın? — When did you go outside?
  • Yemek yedikten sonra. — After eating.

In the exercises, you'll practise building the correct -DIktan sonra form from different verb stems and using it to link two actions in the right time order.

title: Future-in-the-Past
explanation:
The future-in-the-past talks about something that was going to happen at some point, regardless of whether it actually did. English does exactly the same thing with "was/were going to..." — so the concept itself isn't new, just the Turkish form.

It's built by combining the future suffix -ecek/-acak (which you already know) with the past tense of the copula, -di. In other words, you take a normal future-tense verb and just add the past ending onto the end of it.

The suffix has four forms depending on vowel harmony and voicing, same as the regular past tense:

  • -ecekti (front, unvoiced-final e.g. gel-)
  • -acaktı (back, unvoiced-final e.g. bak-)
  • -eceğ+di → -ecekti for most stems (the k softens to ğ before a vowel, but here -ti keeps it as k — see note below)

Basic examples:

  • gelecekti = he/she was going to come
  • gidecektim = I was going to go
  • yapacaktık = we were going to do (it)
  • görecektin = you were going to see

Note on the consonant: the future suffix's -k softens to -ğ- only when followed by a vowel (like the personal ending -im in gideceğim, "I will go"). But the past copula -di starts with a consonant, so no softening happens — the k stays exactly as it is: gidecek + ti → gidecekti.

Personal endings attach after -ti/-tı, just like the simple past tense:

  • gelecektim = I was going to come
  • gelecektin = you were going to come
  • gelecekti = he/she was going to come
  • gelecektik = we were going to come
  • gelecektiniz = you (plural) were going to come
  • gelecektiler = they were going to come

Examples in full sentences:

  • Gelecekti ama gelmedi. = He was going to come, but he didn't.
  • Sana yardım edecektim. = I was going to help you.
  • Yağmur yağacaktı, yağmadı. = It was going to rain, but it didn't.
  • Onu arayacaktık, unuttuk. = We were going to call him, we forgot.

The whole point of this tense is the contrast it sets up: something was planned or expected, but the sentence usually goes on to say it didn't happen (or at least implies some twist). You'll very often see it paired with ama (but) or a follow-up clause explaining what actually occurred.

This is different from the converb -meden you just learned, which links two actions of the same subject in one sentence ("without/before doing"); future-in-the-past instead stands alone as a full predicate describing an unrealized (or not-yet-confirmed) plan.

In the exercises, you'll practise building future-in-the-past forms with the right vowel harmony and personal endings, and using them to express plans that fell through.

title: Verbal Nouns
explanation:
Turkish can turn any verb into a noun, letting it act as the subject or object of a sentence — much like English "-ing" nouns ("the going", "the singing") or words like "arrival", "departure". This is called a verbal noun, and it replaces English gerunds and many "the act of..." constructions.

There are two common verbal-noun suffixes, and they don't always mean quite the same thing.

  • -me / -ma (front/back harmony) — the abstract, grammatical "act of doing X"
  • -iş / -ış / -uş / -üş (four-way harmony) — often more concrete, and frequently lexicalised as its own everyday word

Basic examples:

  • gitme = the going / the act of going
  • gidiş = the departure
  • gelme = the coming
  • geliş = the arrival
  • okuma = the reading (also: "a reading", as in a book reading)

1. -me/-ma is the productive, all-purpose choice. You can build it from almost any verb, and it usually functions like a plain gerund — the direct grammatical equivalent of "doing X":

  • yüzmek → yüzme = to swim → swimming (e.g. yüzme havuzu = swimming pool)
  • beklemek → bekleme = to wait → waiting (e.g. bekleme odası = waiting room)
  • koşmak → koşma = to run → running

2. -iş/-ış/-uş/-üş is less predictable and often has its own specific, narrower meaning. Both nouns can exist from the same root, but they drift apart in usage:

  • gitmek → gidiş = to go → the departure/the trip there (note: t softens to d, as usual before a vowel)
  • gülmek → gülüş = to laugh → a laugh/way of laughing
  • bakmak → bakış = to look → a look/glance

Because of this, it's best to learn each -iş form as its own vocabulary item rather than assuming it always matches the plain "-ing" sense of -me.

Examples in full sentences:

  • Erken kalkma bana zor geliyor. = Getting up early is hard for me.
  • Onun gülüşünü seviyorum. = I like his/her laugh.
  • Sigara içmek yasaktır. — literally "the act of smoking" using the infinitive form, but içme also appears in compounds like içme suyu = drinking water.
  • Gidişin çok ani oldu. = Your departure was very sudden.
  • Yüzmeyi seviyorum. = I like swimming. (verbal noun yüzme takes the accusative -yi here as the object of "seviyorum")

Notice that last example: once a verb has been turned into a noun with -me, it behaves exactly like any other noun — it can take case suffixes such as the accusative (-yi), possessive endings, or the genitive, just like ev or kitap would.

This is different from the tenses you've studied so far, like the future-in-the-past, where the verb stays a verb and simply carries a different time meaning. Here, the verb stops being a verb altogether and becomes a real noun that can be the subject, object, or even take further suffixes.

In the exercises, you'll practise building both verbal-noun forms from familiar verbs and using them correctly as subjects or objects in a sentence.

title: Converb -Ip (Sequential Actions)
explanation:
The -Ip converb links two or more actions done by the same subject, roughly like English "and" between verbs — "went and got," "took and came." Instead of repeating tense and person on every verb, Turkish only marks the last verb fully; the earlier verb(s) just take the bare -Ip suffix and borrow the tense/person from the final verb.

Like other converbs, -Ip attaches directly to the verb stem and follows four-way vowel harmony:

  • -ıp (after a, ı)
  • -ip (after e, i)
  • -up (after o, u)
  • -üp (after ö, ü)

Basic examples:

  • gidip = going (and then)... (from gitmek)
  • alıp = taking (and then)... (from almak)
  • gelip = coming (and then)... (from gelmek)
  • bakıp = looking (and then)... (from bakmak)

The -Ip verb itself carries no tense and no person ending — it's a "naked" stem plus the suffix. All of that information arrives only once, on the final verb of the chain:

  • gidip aldım = I went and got (it) — literally "going, I-got"
  • alıp geldi = he/she took (it) and came
  • yıkanıp giyindim = I washed up and got dressed
  • oturup konuştuk = we sat down and talked

You can chain more than two verbs the same way — every verb except the last stays in the -Ip form:

  • kalkıp yıkanıp gitti = he got up, washed up, and left

The subject must be the same across all the linked verbs. If the subject changes, you can't use -Ip — you need separate clauses instead:

  • Eve gidip yemek yaptım. = I went home and made food. (same person did both)
  • ✗ not used when subjects differ, e.g. "I went home and she cooked" needs a different construction.

Compare with -DIktan sonra from the previous lesson: both link two actions by the same subject, but -DIktan sonra stresses that the first action is fully finished before the second starts ("after doing"), while -Ip is more neutral and often suggests the actions flow together as one continuous sequence — gittikten sonra aldım (after I went, I got it — more deliberate) vs. gidip aldım (I went and got it — a smooth, connected sequence).

Full-sentence examples:

  • Markete gidip ekmek aldım. = I went to the market and bought bread.
  • Kalkıp pencereyi açtı. = He/she got up and opened the window.
  • Çalışıp para kazanıyor. = He/she works and earns money.
  • Elini yıkayıp sofraya oturdu. = He/she washed his/her hand(s) and sat down at the table.

In the exercises, you'll practise forming -Ip chains from verb pairs and choosing when a shared subject allows you to link actions this way instead of repeating tense and person on each verb.

title: Converb: "When" (-diğinde)
explanation:
The -diğinde converb means "when X happens/happened" — it packs an entire English "when..." clause into a single suffixed verb form. There's no separate word for "when" inside the clause; the suffix does all the work.

You already met the -dik/-dığ verbal noun ending in the previous lesson (the "fact that" form used with possessive suffixes, as in geldiğim = "my coming/that I came"). This converb is built from exactly that same verbal noun, plus a possessive suffix for the person doing the action, plus the locative -de/-da ("in/at/on") glued on the end — literally "at the [person]'s -ing", which Turkish uses idiomatically to mean "when [person] -s/-ed".

The core piece -dik follows four-way vowel harmony and consonant softening (k→ğ after vowels), just like the verbal noun:

  • -diğinde (after e, i)
  • -dığında (after a, ı)
  • -duğunda (after o, u)
  • -düğünde (after ö, ü)

Basic examples with the third-person possessive (-i/-ı/-u/-ü, "he/she/it"):

  • gel + diğinde → geldiğinde = when he/she comes/came
  • bak + tığında → baktığında = when he/she looks/looked (k→ hard, no softening after unvoiced consonants)
  • oku + duğunda → okuduğunda = when he/she reads/read
  • gör + düğünde → gördüğünde = when he/she sees/saw

Because it's possessive-based, you can also mark who does the action by swapping the possessive ending:

  • geldiğimde = when I come/came (-im, "my")
  • geldiğinde = when you come/came (-in, "your") — note this looks identical to the "he/she" form; context tells them apart
  • geldiğimizde = when we come/came (-imiz, "our")

Notice this suffix doesn't change for tense the way normal verbs do — the same -diğinde form covers both "when he arrives" (present/future) and "when he arrived" (past); the surrounding sentence's own tense tells you which is meant.

Examples in full sentences:

  • Eve geldiğinde beni ara. = When you get home, call me.
  • Ali eve geldiğinde yemek hazırdı. = When Ali arrived home, the food was ready.
  • Onu gördüğümde çok şaşırdım. = When I saw him, I was very surprised.
  • Hava soğuduğunda kapıyı kapatırım. = When the weather gets cold, I close the door.

In the exercises, you'll practise attaching -diğinde with the correct vowel harmony, consonant softening, and possessive person, and using it to build natural "when..." sentences without a separate word for "when".

title: Converb: "As Soon As" (-ınca)
explanation:
The suffix -ınca attaches directly to a verb stem to mean "as soon as / when [that happens]." It's a converb — a verb form that works like a built-in time clause, so you don't need a separate word for "when" at all.

This suffix follows four-way vowel harmony (ı/i/u/ü) and has no tense marking or personal ending of its own — the time and subject are understood from context and the main clause that follows.

  • -ınca (after a, ı)
  • -ince (after e, i)
  • -unca (after o, u)
  • -ünce (after ö, ü)

Basic examples:

  • varınca = as soon as (he/she/it) arrives
  • gelince = as soon as (he/she/it) comes
  • duyunca = as soon as (he/she/it) hears
  • görünce = as soon as (he/she/it) sees

Word-building examples:

  • var + ınca → varınca = arrive + as.soon.as → as soon as he/she arrives
  • gel + ince → gelince = come + as.soon.as → as soon as he/she comes
  • oku + yunca → okuyunca = read + as.soon.as → as soon as he/she reads (buffer -y- added between two vowels)

Full sentence examples:

  • Okula varınca beni ara. = As soon as you get to school, call me.
  • Haberi duyunca çok sevindim. = As soon as I heard the news, I was very happy.
  • Yemek pişince yiyeceğiz. = As soon as the food is cooked, we'll eat.
  • Onu görünce tanıdım. = As soon as I saw him/her, I recognized him/her.

Just like -diğinde from the previous lesson, -ınca replaces an English "when" clause without needing a separate conjunction — the whole idea of "when X happens" is packed into the verb itself. The difference is one of feel: -diğinde is neutral about timing ("when/at the time that"), while -ınca pushes toward immediate sequence ("as soon as, right after"). In many everyday sentences, native speakers use them almost interchangeably, so don't worry too much about picking the "perfect" one.

In the exercises, you'll practice attaching -ınca correctly to different verb stems (with the right vowel harmony and buffer -y- where needed) and using it to build "as soon as" sentences.

title: The Diminutive -cik
explanation:
The diminutive suffix -cik makes something smaller, cuter, or softer. It's similar to how English adds "-y" or "-ie" to soften a word (dog → doggy, tiny → teeny), or adds "just a little" to soften a request.

-cik follows full four-way vowel harmony (and consonant harmony), so it has eight possible forms:

  • -cik (after front unrounded vowels: e, i)
  • -cık (after back unrounded vowels: a, ı)
  • -cük (after front rounded vowels: ö, ü)
  • -cuk (after back rounded vowels: o, u)

After a voiceless consonant (ç, f, h, k, p, s, ş, t), the "c" devoices to "ç": -çik / -çık / -çük / -çuk.

Basic examples:

  • kedi (cat) → kedicik = kitty
  • az (little) → azıcık = just a tiny bit
  • küçük (small) → küçücük = teeny-tiny
  • kız (girl) → kızcık = little girl (dear)
  • ev (house) → evcik = little house, cottage

Notice azıcık: a buffer vowel "ı" is inserted between "az" and "cık" because "az" ends in a consonant and adding the suffix directly would create an awkward cluster — this happens with a handful of short roots like az and bir (biricik, "one and only, precious").

Some words also double a consonant or shift slightly for sound reasons — these are worth learning as fixed forms rather than deriving from a rule: bir → biricik (one and only), küçük → küçücük (teeny), az → azıcık (a tiny bit).

Examples in full sentences:

  • Azıcık bekle. = Wait just a little bit.
  • Kedicik çok tatlı. = The kitty is very sweet.
  • Küçücük bir ev aldık. = We bought a teeny-tiny house.
  • Bana biraz su ver, azıcık yeter. = Give me some water, just a little is enough.

-cik is very common in affectionate, informal, or child-directed speech — it softens requests, shows fondness for people or animals, and can make an amount feel smaller and less demanding, much like adding "just a little" or "-y" in English. Unlike the converb -ınca, which builds a clause meaning "as soon as," -cik attaches directly to nouns and adjectives to change their feel rather than to link two actions.

In the exercises, you'll practise recognising and forming diminutive words with the correct vowel-harmony variant, including the buffer vowel in words like azıcık.

title: Participles
explanation:
In English, relative clauses use words like "who," "which," or "that": the man who came, the book that I read. Turkish doesn't have relative pronouns at all — instead, it turns the whole verb into an adjective-like form called a participle, which sits directly in front of the noun it describes.

This means the entire relative clause is squeezed into a single word before the noun, in the opposite order from English. It takes practice, but once it clicks, it's very efficient.

There are two main participle types you'll use constantly:

  • -en/-an (subject participle: the noun is the one doing the action)
  • -diğim/-duğum etc. (object participle: the noun is the one having the action done to it, with a possessive suffix showing who did it)

Basic examples with -en/-an:

  • gelen adam = the man who is coming/came (lit. "coming man")
  • okuyan çocuk = the child who reads/is reading
  • uyuyan kedi = the sleeping cat

Here, the noun (adam, çocuk, kedi) is the subject of the verb — the man himself comes, the child himself reads. No tense marker is needed; context tells you whether it's present or past.

1. The object participle (-dik/-diğim) is trickier because the noun is not doing the action — someone else is, and that someone is marked with a possessive suffix glued onto the participle itself.

  • oku + duk + um → okuduğum kitap = read + [participle] + my → the book that I read (lit. "my-read book")
  • gör + dük + ün → gördüğün film = the film that you saw (lit. "your-seen film")
  • yap + tık + ı → yaptığı iş = the job that he/she did (lit. "his/her-done job")

Notice the final -k softens to -ğ before the possessive suffix (duk→duğ, tık→tığ) — the same kind of consonant softening you may have noticed elsewhere in Turkish suffixes.

Full-sentence examples:

  • Gelen adamı tanıyorum. = I know the man who is coming.
  • Okuduğum kitap çok güzeldi. = The book I read was very good.
  • Dün gördüğün film neydi? = What was the film you saw yesterday?
  • Yaptığı iş zordu. = The job he/she did was hard.

A handy way to think about it: ask yourself whether the noun is the doer of the verb (use -en/-an) or the receiver of the verb, with someone else doing it (use -dik + possessive). Once you can tell those apart, choosing the right participle becomes automatic.

In the exercises, you'll practise building both participle types and unpacking them back into natural English relative clauses.

title: Compound Past Combinations
explanation:
You already know two ways to talk about the past in Turkish: -di (the definite past, for things you witnessed or know for certain) and -miş (the hearsay/inferential past, for things you heard about or deduced). Turkish lets you stack these together to build a "past of the past" — a compound tense that works much like the English past perfect ("had gone," "had done").

The core combination you'll meet in this lesson is -miş + -ti, glued onto the verb stem in that order:

  • git-miş-ti = he had (apparently) gone
  • gel-miş-ti = he had (apparently) come
  • yap-mış-tı = he had (apparently) done [it]
  • ye-miş-ti = he had (apparently) eaten

The -miş part still carries its usual flavor: the speaker didn't witness the event directly, but is reporting it secondhand or inferring it from evidence. The -ti part pushes the whole thing further back in time, into a past-before-a-past. Together they answer: "what had already happened, as far as I've heard/gathered, before some other past moment?"

1. Both parts follow their own vowel harmony rules, independently. The -miş suffix has four forms (miş/mış/muş/müş, matching the last vowel of the stem), and the -ti that follows it also harmonizes to two-way front/back agreement (ti/tı/tu/tü) and devoices to -ti/-tı/-tu/-tü vs -di/-dı/-du/-dü depending on the preceding consonant — but since -miş always ends in ş (a voiceless consonant), the following copula is always the voiceless t-form:

  • gör + müş + tü → görmüştü = he had (apparently) seen
  • oku + muş + tu → okumuştu = he had (apparently) read
  • kal + mış + tı → kalmıştı = he had (apparently) stayed

2. The compound conjugates for person just like any past tense, by adding personal endings after -ti/-tı/-tu/-tü:

  • gitmiştim = I had (apparently) gone
  • gitmiştin = you had (apparently) gone
  • gitmiştik = we had (apparently) gone

Examples in full sentences:

  • Ben eve gittiğimde, o çoktan yemek yapmıştı. = When I got home, she had already made food.
  • Duydum ki, sen de o filmi izlemiştin. = I heard that you had watched that movie too.
  • Biz varmadan önce tren kalkmıştı. = The train had (already) left before we arrived.
  • Onlar daha önce hiç İstanbul'a gitmemişti. = They had never been to Istanbul before.

This connects nicely to the participles you just learned: a participle like gittiği ("that he went / his going") often sets the reference point in time, and the compound past then tells you what had already happened relative to it — as in the first example above, where eve gittiğimde sets the moment, and yemek yapmıştı describes what had already occurred by then.

This is genuinely advanced material, since it layers two suffix systems you've only recently mastered on top of each other — take it slowly and lean on the individual -di and -miş rules you already know.

In the exercises, you'll practise building and recognising these "past of the past" forms, and using them to describe one past event that had already finished before another past event happened.

title: Light Verb Constructions (etmek/olmak/yapmak)
explanation:
Turkish borrowed a huge number of nouns from Arabic and Persian (words like yardım "help", teşekkür "thanks", hasta "sick"), and instead of turning them into single verbs, Turkish just pairs them with a small set of helper verbs. These pairings are called light verb constructions: a noun/adjective + a "light" verb that carries almost no meaning of its own, but supplies the tense, person, and grammar.

The three main light verbs are:

  • etmek = "to do" (used with borrowed action-nouns)
  • yapmak = "to do/make" (used with some native and borrowed action-nouns)
  • olmak = "to become/be" (used with adjectives/states to show a change)

Basic examples:

  • yardım etmek = to help (literally "to do help")
  • teşekkür etmek = to thank (literally "to do thanks")
  • hasta olmak = to become sick
  • mutlu olmak = to become happy
  • banyo yapmak = to take a bath (literally "to do bath")

These act as a single unit, but only the light verb conjugates — the noun/adjective in front stays frozen:

  • Sana yardım ediyorum. = I am helping you.
  • Teşekkür ederim. = I thank you. (the standard way to say "thank you")
  • Hasta oldum. = I became sick.
  • Yardım etti. = He/she helped.

Choosing the right light verb isn't always predictable, so it's best to learn each pairing as a fixed phrase rather than trying to derive it from a rule. A few guiding patterns still help:

1. etmek pairs with borrowed action-nouns, especially from Arabic/Persian, describing an action being carried out:

  • yardım etmek = to help
  • hitap etmek = to address (speak to)
  • kabul etmek = to accept

2. olmak pairs with adjectives or nouns describing a state, and marks a change into that state — much like English "become":

  • hasta olmak = to become sick
  • yorgun olmak = to become/be tired
  • öğretmen olmak = to become a teacher

3. yapmak pairs with concrete activities, closer to English "do/make":

  • banyo yapmak = to take a bath
  • alışveriş yapmak = to go shopping
  • spor yapmak = to do sports
